At this intermediate season of the year, wheN things as regards dress are practically at standstill, and there are few innovations in the sartorial world worthy of note, we are princi. pally occupied in the task of making the clothes we now possess present as smart an aspect as possible for the next few weeks till fashions for early winter will become more pronounced, This summer there have been wonderfully few days when muslin and laces could be worn, and this it must be confessed is a matter of deep re- gret; for never before, I fancy, were there so many charming colours and patterns proffered for our selection at very moderate prices. Muslins in particular have been most dainty and . allur- ing, and have lent themselves so kindly to the prevailing modes of this season. However, it is a comfort to reflect that these lovely frocks are not wasted, nor need they be put aside to another year, when they are sure to be a little out of date, as by removing the lace yoke and adding a frill of soft lace and a knot of ribbons or flowers, they can be made to do duty for the simpler evening toilettes. Here, for instance, is de- picttd a very pretty gown of clear white muslin

div.head: PRETTY DRESS.
div.p: A PRETTY DRESS.

sprigged with forget-me-nots which has been transformed by a few tasteful and simple alterations into a really i elegant evening toilette. The yoke having been removed, the decolletage is softened by one of the wide lace collars so fashionable at present, which can be bought ready made, or can be manufactured at home out of piece lace by aid of a paper pattern at a much smaller cost. The collar is embellished by three lines of very narrow pale blue satin ribbon, interthreaded through the pattern of the lace. The front of the bodice where the two points of the collar meet is finished off by a bunch ;of forget-me-nots tied with some of the narrow pale blue ribbon, while the waist is completed by a satin-sash of, the same shade of ribbon finishing at the back in a dainty butterfly bow. The sleeves are cut short and only reach to the elbow, where a full frill of lace of the same pattern as the collar falls over the arms. A little twist of satin ribbon finishes the join between the lace and the muslin. A twist of ribbon through the coiffeure or a bunch ,of flowers in the hair, and, with some dainty shoes and gloves, the otherwise discarded summer toilette is ready to brave all criticism in its new character as an evening gown.

The-ca-pe sketched is of an exceedingly simple style, but forms one of the most useful out-door wraps one could possess at this season of the year, as it can be so easily slipped off or on. It is made in this instance of good warm cloth sufficiently heavy to be worn unlined. There are many materials of this description sold for

div.head: USEFUL CAI'E:
div.p: A USEFUL CAI'E:

the purpose, some of which have a tartan or checked pattern on the wrong side. It is best, when making a wrap of this description one's self, to select a heavy material, as otherwise a lining of some sort is necessary and will add greatly to the difficulties of the amateur worker. The cape sketched is of navy blue stuff with a light brownish checked lining of a large pattern two yards of the cloth `only being required as it is very wide, being fifty-two inches. The pattern for such a cape is very simple as there is only one seam in it, down the centre of the back. In finishing off the edges of the cape it is, of course, impossible to turn in a hem as the material is so thick. Therefore finish in instead with a piece of sarsenet ribbon or Prussian binding. Very large buttons fasten the cape in front. Some people prefer the loose coats to a cal*, and they certainly have many advantages, as they do not blow up in a gale cf wind. Blue is a colour much worn at present for woollen fabrics, and is generally becoming. In linen and foulard it k also a popular tone. The newest shades havd.lmore of the true royal tone. The charming hat illustrated is of dark blue, straw trimmed with bright red velvet ribbon and cherries, a pleasing combination of colours and one which could be worn far on into the year. Flat hats are still fashionable, trimmed with fruit of one kind or another. The Lam- bolle shape which is bent down over the face in front and over the hair at the back is to my mind a rather trying shape to most faces, although one .sees it constantly worn. It is

• generally trimmed with fruit, and has long loops of ribbon hanging half way down the back of the wearer. Felt hats are only beginning to make their debut, but those individuals who travel much are already possessed of a sr-..art shape. It is noticeable, however, that though each ensuing season sees its special novelty in felt hats there are one or two shapes. which newer go out of fashion and are always smart and becoming. Among these is the boat shape, as it was called in its original form, with a stifling brim trimmed only by a band of ribbon and one or two quills. This season there will be some very picturesque varieties adorned witb sweeping ostrich plumes.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY SEPTEMBER 19 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY SEPTEMBER 19 1902
WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Ductless of Albany, who has been living oa the Continent for the past two or three years, in ceder to look after her son, intends to take up her residence again at Claremont. The mansion was the private pro- pene of Queen Victoria, just the same as Osborne and Balmoral, and was left to the Duchees by her late Majesty. It was settled on the daughter of George IV, who married Prince Leopold, the first King of the Bel- gians. Afterwards he sold the property to Queen Victoria. though for considerably less than it oost Lord Clive, who built the present house at a cost of over £lOO,OOO. ' What the bagpipes are in Sootlend ,so ii the harp in Wales, where certain families retain the services of a 'private harpist, who is the counterpart of the private piper in Scotland. In Wales however, much more &nen- ' tien is given to vocal music, and chorus singing is as popular amongst the Welsh as it is amongst the Tyrc- leans in Switzerland. The Royal National Eisteddfod is chiefly concerned in granting degrees to aspirants to musical and rootic henours, though in recent times its patronage has been extended to other arts, and even to such domestic employment as weaving, embroidery,and sewing. Altogether,the prizes offered at the Eisteddfod at Bangor this year amounted to close upon £l,OOO. The Coronation year has been prolific in disappoint- ' meats, one of which was the failure of M. Santos Dumont t, give a demonstration of his air-ship in Landon. One of the sights of Coronation week, was to 11 have been his attempt from the Crystal Palace, to sail round the dome of St. Paul's Cathedral, but something happened to his machinery and nothing more was heard about it. But M. Santos Dumont is still busy with hie projects, and announces that in two months time he will start a regular mrial service in Paris. A booking office will be opened, and applications are already being made for tickets. Fares will be high, in a double sense, but that will not prevent people in indulging in risky foolish- ness, until some awful tragedy compels the law to step In and put a stop to it. Women have to take the ordinary [lgo of life but how frequently we are reminded that our style of dress is designed to court dangers, It is especially liable to catch fire, and to cause other accidents,such as falle,and to generally place us at a disadvantage. A lighted match thrown dawn by a careless smoker has frequently set a woman's dress on fire, and this was the cause only the other day of the death of s girl at Cardiff. A wan may pass over a lighted match without any riiak, but a summer frock is instantly ret in a blaze, and similar dangers attach to women's clothing in the house. It is therefore scarcely surprising that those who advocate the reform of women's dress should make tho most of these points, but it is all to no avail, and what life that movement ever had seems to have died out in recent years. There is nothing like dust and mud for ruining one's clothes, and any means of banishing these drayrbacks from the highways would be a boon to women. But the idea of gaining this end by oiling the roadways seems a little risky. Mud is bad en eagle, but this mixed with oily particles would mean absolute ruination to the roughest of wear, to say nothing about light summer toilettes. ,In San Francisco, and also in the Riviera, the experiment of oiling the driveways has been tried, and found that it makes them smooth and free from dust, and except for a slight odour of petroleum, perfectly agreeable. The process seems to answer very well in those parts which enjoy a long dry summer season,where the sun bakes the roadway int* a hard, smooth, and waterproof surface, but the result has not been so satis- factory in places where rain frequently falls all the year round. It would therefore hardly seem likely that it would succeed in this country, though the experiment is to be tried in one of the southern counties, and cyclists and sutomobilists will watch the result with no little interest. _ _ _ _ .

A novelty, is the placing of chiffon sleeves, into the smartest cloth gowns. The begging arrangement still reigns supreme, but In the heavier autumn fabrics the Idea Is far from successful—hence the introduction of chiffon fee this purpose. Sometimes the entire sleeve from the" cap " downwards to the wrist, is of chiffon at others it Is only the lower part of the sleeve that is thus lightened. In almost every instance however, the ehlfen is Incrusted with lace. er better still, cicth, aotife, thus blending the oettume into one harmonious whole.

Tbe crsze for tassels and cards, promises to be short lived, already they are appearing in the cheap, and con- sequently nasty varieties. Buttons have already taken their place, on many of the smartest gowns, coats, and mantles, sometimes being very large aud flat, and covered in velvet, or crochet, at others quite smell, and let closely in rows. Hundreds of these quite small buttons are employed to trim a fashionable gown, and the effect in many instances is particularly good. We are, happily, determined not to muffle our necks this autumn. The big, round fur boas, which were answerable for many a sore and weak throat, have dis- appeared, so has the storm cellar, also the plain military collar band we indulged in last winter. Coats and mantles are chewing tie collar at all, the neck Niue cut down allgh9y, and sot into a piece of velvet or embroid- ery. The fiat detachable fur pelerine can, as winter advances, be more easily worn over thie a,rangeooent, and when this is not necessary, a stack will afford con- siderable warmth. The new casement liners are really very excellent materials for the purpose, and are procurable in many coleurs. There are several shades of green to be had, beside blues, beffe, heliotropes, and reds, none of these crude, but subdued in tone, to assert well with the arrangement of almost any room. One of the latest ideas for using casement linen for high pitched sash windows is particularly good. Short blinds of plain coloured linen are run on a rod, so as to epen or close as desired over the lower sash, while there are long side curtains topped by a full frill, and made of the same fabric printed. The plain and pattern materials together have an excellent effect. It is claimed that these linens hang and wear well, that they keen their colour, and are not costly. Further they are soft and yielding, and the lighter tones veil without entirely excluding the light. Housewives should be careful of mbar,/ cheap enamelled utensils for cooleine, as the soft and inferior enamels are liable to give off such deadly poisons as arsenic, lead, and antimony. Instances have occurred in which home- made jam. boiled in such vessels, has made those par- taking of it violently ill,and investigation has traced the contamination to the enamel of the saucepan. An easy test of this kind of holloware is to boil a strong solution of common salt cr soda in it, and if It takes the glaze ff the enamel it is net fit to be need for cooking pur- poses. A hard, good enamel is unaffected by these experiments and only articles of the better quality should be allowed in the kitchen. MADGE.

Another Runaway. Horse at Warrington.

• About noes Si Saturday a horse and trap belong- ing to Mr Edward Connor were standing in Price- street while the driver bad gone into his house for dinner. The animal it is supposed was frightened by the noise caused by an eagine passing some where in the neighbourhcod, and belted off down Beweey- street into Horsemarket-street. Here a men named James Rothwell, a market salesman, succeeded in getting hold of the reins,but the horse got away and the man was thrown down,one of the wheels of the vehicle passing over his shoulder. The horse proceeded a law yards further when it was stopped by Mr Lowe,of Sankey Hall Farra,with the assistance of a young man whose name the police have not been able to ascertain. No damage was done to the trap, but Rothwell was badly shaken and his clothes tern.

THE HOUSE ON THE HILL,
BT G. B. BURGIN. (Author of "A Quaker Girl," &c., &c.)
PART I.

Isabel Archer daintily crossed the Gray's Inn Road. After breathing a devout little prayer of thankfulness that she had not been offered up to the deity who presides over the trains there, she surveyed her muddy skirts with an expression of refined disgust. "There is nothing like London mud," she mused, "to make a girl feel that she belongs to the lowly ones of the earth. I suppose this is the entrance to Verulam Buildings. Let me look round so that I shall know it again." She looked round. Then she drew a slip of paper from her pocket and consulted it. "No. 122, Verulam Buildings," she said, narrowly escaping the charge of a British workman who was bearing down on her with a window-frame. "Now for Messrs. Perkins, Snoop, and Dilwater." She entered No. 122. One of the walls bore a legend to the effect that the offices of Messrs. Perkins, Snoop, and Dilwater were the first pair back. She sprang lightly up the stbne steps, only to be confronted by a statement that all parcels for the firm were to be left in the basement with the porter. "I am not a parcel for the firm," said Isabel, decidedly, "and I will not be left in the basement. Stay, here is a bell. I will beard Messrs. Perkins, Snoop and Dilwater in their den. Why, even their door is sticky with paint." She pulled the rusty bell-handle, which somehow or other had been overlooked in the general thirst for rejuvenating this venerable pile. The echoes died away. She rang again. No reply. At the third pull, the door opened suddenly, and a small voice entreated her to stow it." When Isabel recovered from her astonishment, she looked round for the owner of the voice. She found him in a corner, seated on a stool. He was a small youth with a big head, which was half buried in a thrilling romance of the blood-and- thunder order. There was a highly-imaginative drawing of a trapper knocking Indians down with the butt-end of a rifle, and in the foreground several other white men were busily engaged scalping' "Lo, the poor Indian." " Ah, ' said the little boy, fondly contemplating this work of art, "that's gory, that is—real Buffalo Bill."

He tore himself reluctantly away from the paper, and dropped the string with which he had opened the door. Perhaps you will have the goodness to attend to me," said Isabel, somewhat sharply. The mud had tried her temper. "Put down that rubbish at once."
The small boy put down the paper, and wheeled his stool round until it rested on one leg. "What can I do for you, madam ? "he said, in obvious imitation of someone else.
" You can answer my questions," said Isabel, peering into the den, the sole inhabitant of which appeared to be the juvenile spider before her. "I want to see Mr. Perkins." _ _

" Kensal Green," said the small boy, deeply resenting her tone. "First turning to the left after the entrance. Marble moniment and gera- niums. Res urgam." " Dead ? " queried Isabel. The small boy nodded. "As a herring," he said:
Isabel consulted the slip of paper. "Well, then, Mr. Snoop ? " " Finchley," said the small boy. "Ask the lodge-keeper. Plain cross and lobelia. Deeply lamented.' _ _ _
habel began to feel frightened. There was something uncanny about this weird imp. "Mr. Dilwater ?" she queried, in faltering tones, " he—is he alive ?'

The small boy shook his head with proud snportance, yet mournfully withal. "You've not seard ?" he asked. "Heard? No." "Went to Greece for the vacation. Shot by the Brigands. Requiesca.t in pieces. We've got one of his ears and his easy chair. Like to sit in it.?" Isabel felt faint. "Do—do their ghosts attend to business?" she asked, in the manner of one on the eve of a great discovery to be communicated to the Psychical Society. "Who are We'?" "Mr. Dabchick," said the boy. "He and me's all that's left." "And where is the Last of the Barons to be found?" asked Isabel. "I don't know nothing about he Last of the Barone," said the boy. Mr. Dabehick'll be here d'reckly." "And what am I to do in the meantime?"

"Take a walk," said the boy. Something appeared to strike him. " Have-you got an appointment ?" "I have come after one," thought Isabel. "Yes," she said; "but not at Kensal Green Of Finchley." "Then why didn't you say so?" said the Small boy, implying that she had wasted a good deal of his valuable time.

"Because you did'ut ask," said Isabel, hotly. "Show me some place where I can sit down." The small boy descended from his perch. He was older than his size implied.. "Come this way," he said, flinging open a door. Isabel was surprised. She followed the small boy into a spacious apartment, the windows of which looked out into the beautiful gardens of Gray's Inn. Not a sound could be heard of the traffic only a hundred yards away. Stately limes spread their bending boughs proteetingly over the greensward. Pigeons, rooks, starlings flew about in perfect security; they were under the very eye of the law. The sparrows had lost the perkiness peculiar to their kind, and hopped in as solemn a manner as the Jackdaw of Rheims, after he had felt the withering effects of the Archbishop's curse. Even the cats had a well-fed, prosperous air. The room itself wan bugs, well-furnished, with the customary Turkev. carpet. A few choice engrav- ings hung an The walls. In the frame of one picture, repeesenting a girl listening to a nightin- gale, was a card with Did you hear the nightin- gale sing? A beautiful, silken voice, a web of happy notes, and my soul was taken in its meshes, and strangled and tortured thereby." Isabel paused before the words. "A lawyer who reads Heine is an anomaly," she said. "I am glad he has not gone to Kemal Glen or Finch. ley.' "Thank you," replied a voice behint her. Isabel did not lose her self-possession. She merely turned round and bowed to the new-corner. "It is a bad habit to think aloud," she remarked. "Mr. Dabchiok ? " . _ .

"I am glad you didn't say I presume.' It is so suggestive of Livingstone and Stanley," said the new-coiner, a shrewd, well-dressed, prosperous- looking man of forty, with a rose in his button- hole, and wearing patent leather boots. "I don't like to see a man wearing patent leather boots in the morning," thought Isabel. "In other respects he is presentable." Mr. Dabchick's dark eyes took in Isabel at a glance. "Well-bred, ladylike, and very well dressed," he said to himself. "We ought to be able to come to terms, particularly as I have found out all about her. Won't you take a chair, Miss —" "Archer," said Isabel, filling up the pause. •" Thank you." He went up to the wall, opened a door in the oak panelling, and drew out a blot- ting-pad and some paper. "I like to eliminate all signs of the office,' he said, noting her surprise. "The popular idea of a lawyer is that he has a dull, dark den, wherein he lies in wait, like the

ant-lion at. the bottom of a sand-hollow, so that the unfOctunate ants come tumbling down into his open jams. But we have changed all thit. iWe keep the machinery out of sight as much as possible, when you have once passed the thres- hold."
"Its is not a prepossessing threshold, certainly," said Isabel.
Then there was a pause. "I suppose yea war:ted to talk to me about the advertisement," said Mr. Dabehiek. "'Where did you see it? 'Times?' " " Yes."

_ " Ahra..itvis ,aiways better to put that sort of thing in. the 'Times. Some people are always abusing.am "Tlincs' because it is old-fashioned." But:about:this appointment," suggested Isabel. "Oh, yes," said Mr. Dabchick, as if the subject really didn't matter. "It's for a middle-aged lady,.a client of mine, who wants a companion." I "In the country or town?" 1 "In the country." He seemed to think he had given all the information necessary. "But ).that am! expected to do?" asked the
puzzled Isabel, lifting-her dark eyelashes in the direction of Ilr. Dabchick. _ .

Mr. Dabchick toyed with his paper-knife in a listless fashion. "There really isn't much to do," he said, "except to be with her more or less. Ride, drive, play, see that the housemaid darns stockings, and all that sort of thing. You've plenty of nerve?"

"Oh yes. Why?" "Lonely:sort of place," said Mr. Dabohick, "right away in Derbyshire, not far from Chatsworth. No society, except Geoffrey Hearne." "And who is Geoffrey Hearne ? " "He looks after the estate," said Mr. Dabohick. "Oh, there is an estate." "Yes. Miss Summerby owns a lot of land be- sides the House on the

This was a,little more explanatory. "Of course, you would expect an adequate com- pensation for going to a place like that," said Mr. Dabchick. "Would a hundred a year be suf- ficient?" He said it in a tone which implied that money was no object. "A hundred a year would do very well," said Isabel.

"It would to dress on," said Mr. Dabchick, till more listlessly. "I think I ought to explain," said Isabel. "I am trying this as an experiment. I have no income of my own, and sin living with my mother." "Just so," said Mr. Dabchick, glancing at the heading of the note Isabel had written to the firm. "People can't live in Bryanston Square for nothing. I thought when I got your note that it would be all right, so I made inquiries." Isabel felt rather checkmated. She was prepared to enter into an explanation of the motives which had induced her to leave home. Mr. Dabchick did Rot appear to care to hear them. "Lady Archibald Ellis will be happy to answer any inquiries you may think fit to make," said Isabel.

"Oh yes, quite so. I don't think it will be necessary," said Mr. Dabchick, who prided himself on his iinperturbility. "Ii yea are in search of something new, something which will keep your hands full occasionally, I should think the position would suit you. If you don't like it you can always go back to your mother." "When shall I go ?" asked Isabel. .. . .

"Any day next vi7eek," said Dabchick. "You need not hurry. By the way, Miss Summerby is rather puzzling sometimes. You'll understand that when you have been there a little while. Can I offer you a glass of sherry and a biscuit? No? Then I think I need not detain you any, longer." .
"One moment," said Isabel. " People do not offer a hundred a year to a companion without some very good reason. What is the reason in this case ? ' _

said Mr. Dabchick, becoming quietly prompt and hard, "you have divined that. I can't say more. Will, you take your chances?" "Yes I" said Isabel, firmly. I will." " Gripps," called Mr. Dabchick, "the eoor. Good morning, Miss Archer," and Isabel was walking slowly down the Gray's Inn Road before she recovered from her surprise. She felt a new being. "Here is something to live for," she said. "I wonder how mamma will take it."

Mamma took it very calmly. "lb is absurd of you to go away, Isabel," she said. "You will have the money when I die. I think energy is very bad form. I know all about the Summerbys by report." She dismissed the matter from what she was pleased to call her "mind," and went on with her novel. _ _
"Anything is better than this idle, useless life," thought Isabel, abandoning her long tresses to the skilful maid. "It will be a new sensation to do my. own hair." _ . .

he went to bed, and dreamt that Gripps was biting off her ears and burying them in Kemal Green. Some one rescued her from his tenacious grasp. "I am Geoffrey Hearne," said the stranger, and she fell asleep again. Mrs. Archer declined to see Isabel off from St. Pancras. "You have crossed the—l forget the name of the river, but I believe it had something to do with the landing of William the Conqueror, she observed with a sublime, if somewhat hazy, contempt for history. "You have crossed the— oh, yes—Rubicon of your own free will, and I can- not bear to see you go. lam thankful you did not elect to be a lady help. I have escaped that shock. We have much to be thankful for in this world; I hope we shall be spared lady-helps in the next." "Don't be profane, mamma?" said Isabel. "Was I profane?" enquired Mrs. Archer. "I didn't mean to be. All the servants are going off as lady-helps, and it does annoy one. Write and tell me how you get on. There is a hydro- pathic place near Barslow, not far from Chats- worth. I think I will go there in a few months, and then you can come and see me. But I don't expect you will stay at Bedingfield longer than a week. I will tell Perkins to keep your room in readiness. The Ellises want us to go to them when the season is over. I shall hot know how to account for your absence:" .
"Lady Archibald alredy knows all about it," said Isabel.

Then Mrs. Archer solemnly spread out her hands to heaven and gave Isabel up. It is this craving for originality," she moaned, "which is destroying us as a nation. We want to do everything in a different way to everyone else." "I had to give references," said Isabel. The carriage came round, and she departed for Euston.

There was nothing very interesting aboutv-the journey to Derby. She left by the twelve o'clock train, and arrived at Derby a little beyond the usual time. At two o'clock she began to feel hungry, but the manner in which an elderly couple opposite devoured their lunches disgusted her. They simply revelled in the antediluvian fowls supplied in the railway luncheon baskets: They finished their salads with fierce determina- tion, and drank cheap claret with the air of people resolved to have their money's worth. The only other occupant of the carriage, a young fellow of about five-and-twenty, was more interesting. He was tall, fair and well-madb. His tweed travelling suit wasn't new, but looked as if it were thoroughly comfortable. He had a very white forehead, which showed all the more distinctly owing to the hue of a complexion bronzed by exposure to wind and weather. The muscles of his brawny arms were evidently strong as iron bands, to judge.by the way in which he swung a somewhat heavy valise into the rack. Ho appeared to be observant,. for Isabel noticed the look of astonish. ment which spread over his features when one of the elderly travellers swallowed a bluebottle in her claret. "Wonder if it's drowned," he muttered behind his paper, and his shoulders shook. Presently he changed papers with Isabel, and an skilfully mancenvred his own that it shut from her 'sight the gorged and sleepy lunchers. , She felt•grateful to him. It was a piece of good fortune for which she thanked the gods. Younk men were all so very much alike, that it was a relief to her to find one who could display a little originality. They got on very comfortably together. Just before they entered Derby, he electri- fied Isabel by leaning over towards her (he had been looking out of the window rather anxiously, she thought) with "Excuse me for my apparent rudeness,.but-there will be a smash-up directly ;" and beforepshe could reply, he placed her very carefully on the floor, falling on one knee beside her.

The lunchers began to shriek and call for the guard, thinking that they were in the society of a madman, who would cruelly cut their throats before they digested the lunch which had afforded them so much enjoyment. Th 6 muscular youth simply let them take their chances. "Nothing can hurt them after lunch," he mur- mured to Isabel. "They-.--" Wag it 'a chaos? an earthquake? Shouts—cries —a low rumbling sound—then a crash—a clashing of carriages—a shivering shock—splintering glass in all directions—then a gradual silence, only broken by occasional moans... .

"You can,get up now," said the young fellow to Isabel, speaking somewhat huskily. "I thought we were all right, but it was better to take precau- tions. It's not+inneh of a smash. I saw that duffer who is driving the goods train get on the wrong line' and before he could shunt we were into him. It's really nothing when you know it's coming." Isabel got up, feeling rather confused and shaken, but not much the worse for this new experience. It seemed to her that the stranger did not make half enough of it. He appeared to regard it as one of the necessary incidents of travel. "Of course we haven't any insurance tickets," he said, cheerfully. "That is just ray luck. I bought half a dozen papers the last time I went to tewn, ancl.calculated that if I had been smashed I should (or, rather, my people should) have made about two thousand pounds out of it. Some people are always down on their luck." He appeared to regret the absence of papers more than the accident itself. The lunchers clung to him, and entreated to be taken out of the carriage and sent hoine._ They had been severely

sbaken. Tne maws nose bred profusely. Ire thought he was going to die, and moaned out that he wasn't prepared. "Oh, you won't die," said the unknown youth. "If you lived so long after that lunch nothing can hurt you. Of course, you have a flask. They will take our names and addresses directly. I've cut my hand rather badly with the glass." "I owe a great deal to you," said Isabel. She now knew he had arched himself over her and kept away the falling shower of glass from the windows. " Why didn't you try to save the others V' _ : _

"Oh " He made a wry face. "Do people like that deserved to be saved? It was a case of survival of the fittest. Pardon my nonsense, but I wanted to get your nerve back. Here comes the guard." "Anybody hUrt, guard?" he continued, address- ing that worthy. I' " Mftly ribs, sir," said that functionary. "What's the matter with you ? " "Lots. Cut my hand; torn my coat. I shall have a heavy claim against the company." "What name, sir?" "Geoffrey Hearne." "Address?" "The House on the Hill, Bedingfield." "All right, sir. ,And you, Miss?" "Isabel Archer, the House on the Hill, Beding- field."

--Geoffrey Hearne looked at Isabel; Isabel looked at Geoffrey Hearne. "'There's a Providence that shapes our ends,'" said Geoffrey. "Miss Archer, what should I have said to Miss Summerby if I had left you to look after yourself?" He swung his valise down from the rack, and helped Isabel to alight. "We shall just catch the train for M;dingfield," he said, "if we only hurry." To Isabel's utter astonishment her limbs refused to hurry. She sank into a chair, and could not stir. Tears forced themselves into_her eyes; she trembled violently. "You will be all right in a minute," said Geoffrey Hearne, reassuringly. "it's the reaction —that's all. You kept it back, instead of letting yourself go like those people we have just left. I'll get you a glass of sherry." He rushed off, utterly forgetful of his own wants, and soon returned with the sherry. "I don't know whether you would rather have this or another accident," he said ruefully, "hut it was the best I could get. Don't mind if it's rather fiery. It gets fiery on this line at having to wait so long before it is consumed." Isabel drank the sherry, and felt better. "Of course, this thing will be in all the evening papers," said Geoffrey. "Give me the address nf your people, and I will wire them that you are all right. They always get frightened, you know." He was a revelation to Isabel; he seemed to for- get nothing. "Are you not tired yourself?" she said, looking up in amazement. ' "Not a bit." Isabel promptly produced her handkerchief. "Let me see that hand." .

"It is nothing. A little vaseline will put it all right." "Better have it done' sir," said the station. master, hurrying in. "Here's a doctor; he'll make you comfortable." . "All right," said Geoffrey Hearne. "It won't prevent my claiming damages, you know. We'll go into the other room though. It's not a pleasant sight for a lady to witness.' In ten minutes he came back, looking little worse for his adventure. "It seemed to be a nasty cut," said Isabel.
"Well, yes," he admitted reluctantly, "it did bleed a little; but that is healthy. Look at that old chap, Dr. Sargrado, in 'Gil Bias.' He wouldn't have thought anything of it."

This was unanswerable, Isabel knew that the cut was a 'pretty deep one, but she admired the pluck with which he refused to consider it more than a trifle. "We have nearly an hour to wait for the next train," he said. "If you will lie down on the couch here I'll cover you up with this rug, and you'll get a little sleep. It will put your nerves right. Dabchick said that he thought you had plenty of nerve."

He came back in forty minutes to tell her that she had time for a cup of tea. Isabel drank the tea, wondering what manner of man he was to so instinctively divine all that she needed. She felt quite restored, and said so. "Oh yes,," he said, helping her into the carriage. "People make such a fuss about these things. In novels, the girl always faints and, lets down her back hair, and then the hero faints, And she bends over him (how she gets out of her faint they don't say, but she comes out and then goes back again, I suppose), and weeps salt tears which bring him to. Now in real life the whole thing is over directly ; there's no fuss at all. We can't get upset on the way to Bedingfield because it is a branch line, with a single track, and there is only one. train on it."

They started through the darkening shades of night, Isabel feeling drowsily comfortable and not at all disposed to be curious as to when they would reach their journey's end. It really didn't matter. The train sped on through deep cuttings, whose wooded sides hemmed them in. Tall foxgloves nodded and shook their pretty bells to greet her; the wood-pigeons' cooing note camekwith softened melancholy through the night. Little silvery brooks • trickled adown the very verge of the line. Here and there a tall chimney reared its head, but there was no smoke, no noise, no confusion. Only the fresh coolness of the night, and above them the solemn pines and whispering larches. The great full-orbed moon arose, flooding every nook and dell with light. Two or three times they stopped at little stone stations embowered in clustering clematis, the chimneys of which were surrounded by 'trail- ing ivy, whilst grey lichens spotted the slate roofs. As Isabel watched the silvery willows bending to a little wayside stream, Geoffrey Hearne suddenly uttered an 'exclamation. "Look !" he said to Isabel, who was half asleep. " Look I the House on the Hill !"

It stood upon a lonely hillside in the midst of fair gardens—a great, plain, unpretending structure of solemn stone, now softened into tenderness by the loving light of the moon. No trailing flowers hid its rugged outlines. All was bleak, bare, and grim about the House itself. Halfway up the hill it stood, solid, firm, unyielding, scarred by time, seamed here and there as if by lightning blasts. Lonely it was, and rugged to the eye, and yet there was something pathetic, appealing about this ancient haunt. It seemed to say, "Fair gardens lap me round and compass me, giant woods shelter me from the winter storm. Yonder sentinel tower keeps watch and ward, come weal or woe, and yet lam alone. Time touches me not; men come and go—l heed them not. I know all loves and hates and hopes and fears. Children are born beneath my roof; strong men die in me; fair women live and fade away, and I remain unchilled by wintry blast, unscathed by flood and fire; for I am hewn out of the solid rock; strong hands fashioned me; and I endure even as the everlasting hills which gave me birth." Isabel shivered.

Then the train swept round a curve, and drew up at a little station surrounded by flowers. The station-master appeared, bowing low. "Is Kinipple there with the carriage?" asked Geoffrey. "Here I be, sir," said the ruddy-faced Kinipple, touching his hat. "John is aminding the horses outside. We be mortal anxious about the accident, Muster Geoffrey. I'm expecting a young lady, too.''

"Here she is," said Geoffrey, handing Isabel out. "This is Miss Archer, Kinipple." "A Lunnoner, I hope, Miss," said Kinipple. "I be Hertfordshire, I be. But I got lost up here, and I'll never find my way whoam agin." "Not while Mrs. Pilbeam is housekeeper," said Geoffrey; and Kinipple, with a sheepish grin, carried the bags up the steep path to the victoria. , (To be continued. )

div.head: GREAT INCREASE IN FEMALE EMPLOYEES.
div.p: GREAT INCREASE IN FEMALE EMPLOYEES.
Lancashire MAI Statistics.

Some figures quoted by the writer of an article on " Women Workers," in the " Cc-operative News," are full of significance. Taking ten trades, covering spin- ning, weaving, :printing, leather manufactures, furni- ture making, dyeing, watch, toy, and instrument making, manufacture of food, drink, and smoke, paper, dress, earthenware, chemicals, and gas, he finds that in• 1841. they employed 463,600 fen2ales. In 1891 there were 1,447,500 females engaged in them. Wit regard to males, there were workino, in the trules named 1,030,600 in 1841. and in 1891 1,576,100. In 1891, therefore, the women were practically equal in number to the men.
In many of three lines there are features very on pleasant to the workers. 'lke ease of a Blackburn girl need caly be quoted to confirm this.

MSS Martha Mitchell, seventeen years of age,who lives with her parents at 33, John Thoma E-street, Back- burn, suffered a most serious illness which took her away from her comrades at the mill where she worked, small hopes being entertained of her recovery. How- ever she is enjoying robust health again after taking Dr. Williams' pink pil4.

The story of her recovery reada very much like a romance, but it is real enough and is best told in the words of her mother wile, the other day, was inter- viewed on the matter by a reporter of the Blackburn " Standard and Exprese." . _ _

" Yee," said Mr; Mitchell without hesitation, "I attribute my daughter's present good health solely to Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people. Two years ago last November she bad a very bad attack of scarlet fever which left her very weak indeed. Almcst immediately afterwards she got rheumatiern,and for a lorg time could not get about except by crawling on her bands and knees. She continued to be very weak,and we began to think she would never get better. Both myself and hue- band called in the beet doctors we could afford, she was also in the Blacliburia Infirmary, and twelva months ago they sent her to the Convalescent Horne at Southport where she remained for three weeks I ought to have said she was in the Infirmary twice, for it was after her second stay there that they removed her to Southport. She then returned home, but the neighbours all said she was a great way from being right. A few months ago, however, I saw a case in a news- paper of a yeung man,who was seized with rheumatism and I noticed the account said he was cured by taking Dr William's pink pills. I therefore,said to Martha,"we will see what the pills will do for you," and a box of the pills was purchased. . .

- "-She had only taken ths contents of one loci of the pills when I aw she was looking better." " But I felt an improvement right away," interposed the daughter," and it was this feeling of growing well again that encouraged me to continue taking the pills, because you see. I was becoming heartily sick of physics and I should not have kept on with the rills had they not done me good. You see lam quite well now AO that it is a good thing for me that I was gersuaded to try the pills."

" That is perfeetly true," added the mother, " It was not long after she began taking Dr William' pink pills that her appetite commenced to improve, her weakness began to leave her, and she wag able to get about witb- out suffering pain or even fatigue. This happy improve- ment has all been trought about by four boxes of the pills and I can assure yen we are :thankful to see her strong and well again, going about as cheerful as ever. and quite able to follow a hard day's work at the mill." " You knew others then who have benefited from the use of Br William'a pink pills ?" Before Mrs Mitchell had time to reply a neighbour, who had just then entered the house, exclaimed, "yes, she does, for my eon has received much benefit from the pills. We live at 67 in thus street, and my name IS Bradley. My son, some three years ago, b,6 ec, be carried out of the mill owing to illneFs. The Pills and nothing but the pills, cured him,entizely."

THE EDUCATION BILL. Action by the Warrington and Dis- trict Free Church Council. Payment of Rates to be Refused. A meeting of the Warrington and District Free Church Council was held last week in the vestry of the Wesleyan Chapel, Bold-street, to consider what attitude the Council should adopt in respect to the suggested non-payment of the education rate in the event of the Education Bill becomiog law. The proceedings were not open to the press. The circular convening the meeting said :—" An important communication bas been received from the National Council of Frecaurchas respecting the E.tucation Bill. At this important crisis in the hi:tory of Free Churches when their interests are so seriously menaced, it is necessary that such action should be taken as will leave no doubt of the sincerity and intensity of our convictions. As the suggested action is an important one, a frill and representative meeting of the Council is desirable, and your presence is there- fore earnestly requested. Do not fail to be present and laelp:to influence the Government to withdraw; measure which violates both our political and religious prin- ciples." We learn that there was a representative attendance. The President (Mr C E Parker, Penketh) presided. _ Before the circular from the National Council of Free

Churches was considered, the following resolution, moved by the CHAIRMAN. and seconded tw the Rev. J. YONGR, was unanimously adopted This meeting or the Warrington Fred Church Council enters its emphatic protest against the Education Bill now before the coun- try. First, because it seeks before everything else sectarian and priestly ends. Secoud,because it abolishes School Boards, which have done, and are doing,so much for national education, while securing the religious liberty alike of teachers and scholars. Third, because it was introduced, on being forced through Parliament, without any mandate from the nation, the present HOUSR of Commons having been elected for an entirely different and single purpose. Fourth, because it violates the principles of civil and religious liberty by securing the support of denomina- tional schools from public funds _without effective public

control, and by prictioally confining the appointment of teacbe,s in denominational schools to members only of such denominations. This Council, therefore, calls for the absolute withdrawal of the Bi'l, or hereby challenges the Government to appeal to the country on it. It declares its absolute hostility to the measure, and its intention, if the Bill is persisted in, to oppose and thwart its operation to the utmost. Finally, the Coun- cli upon the Free Churchmen of Warrington to stand firm against this glaring attempt to sectarianize national education." The circular from the National Council having been read by the Rev W C J Neville, a discussion followed, and it was resolves, on the raoton of the Rev J F MATTHEWS, seconded by the Rev H Duntaco, " to give an affirmative answer to the question of the National Cannon in regard to the enrolment of the names and addresses of those who feel that they are bound to refuse Payment of the rates levied under this Bill if it should become law, but that the enrolment should be deferred until a later date." The temper nf the meeting was one of uncompromis- ing antagonism to the Bill and of a determined resolution to oppose it. As a further step to the crusade against the Bill the Council unanimously passed the following resolution : " That this Council urges its constituents to refuse to vote for any candidate for the County Borough Council who will not pledge himself to vote apainat carrying out the provisions of this Bill if it becomes law, especi- ally as to levying and collecting the educatian,rate." THE MAYORALTY.

Mr. Parr to be asked to accept Office again. Mr J Carlton Parr is to be asked to accept the office of Mayor for another twelve months. This decision was arrived at at a special meeting of the ' Town Council held on Monday afternoon. Alderman Roberts preeided,and there were also nresent: Alder- en Fnairclough, Sutton. Heaton, Francornb, and sZraltes mvenouncillors Shit!cock, Smathurst,Forshaw, Virilkinaen Tg. Barton, Malkin, Rogers, Greening, . • ohn Roberts Baird A J Jolley. Hulse, rt Duncan. —cnnett John Evans, Davies, Tinnion, William Roberts, Burton, A Jolley, Sampson, and Ellison. A strong wish was expressed that the Mayor would consent to allow his name to be submitted as Mayor for a second vear. Most of the members spoke in high terms of the able manner in which since is election he bad discharged his duties h . on to the civic chair in November last. On the proposition of Alderman SurroNi,secondad by Councillor ELLisoN,it was unanimously resolved that Mr Charlton Parr be cordially invited to accept the offics of Mayor for the ensuing year It was also decided that a memorial be drawn up for pre_ sentation to his worship, expressing the wish of the Council, and that it be presented to him by a de- Imitation consisting of the Deputy-Mayor,Aldermen Sutton, Francomb, and Monks, and Councillor 'Tinnion. We understand that the Mayor is now staying at his Herefordshire seat, Staunton Park, Staunton- on-Arrow, but he will return in time to be present at the dinner to be given on the 25th inst, to the 3rd and 4th contingents of Warrington "Volunteers who have been on active service in South Africa.

Several very interesting articles on the close aesocia- tion between these two conditions will be found in a late number of " The Journal for the Deaf" There is also a good description of a new method of treating catarrhal deafness by external application, which has been so snecesi ful that the editor adds a resume of up- wards of 40 cases cured under his personal observation during the past month. Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was a smaller attendance than usual at the meting of this Society on Sunday. Mr J W Roberts, who was formerly a quarter-master sergeant of the line, occupied the chair, and in ref erring to the scenes which were to be seen so repeatedly in Warrington streets, said there was great need for the P.S.A. movement. There were hundreds of men in Warrington who never went to a place of worship, and he hoped the P.S.A. movement would endeavour to reach some of them and influence them for good. Mr Wilson, of Liverpool, delivered an inspiring address or' the words " Inasmuch as ye have done it to the least of these My brethren ye have done it unto Me." In an interesting way he urged rho mem- bers to let the P.S.A. stand for " power," " service," and " ambition."—The Rev. John Yong° referred to the proposed establishment of a Holiday Savings Club in connection with the society. He pointed nut that in connection with one society in Blackburn £lO,OOO was recently distributed. Be hoped the project would be taken up with enthusiasm by the members.

div.head: Visit to warrington.of the* Wesleyan
div.p: Visit to warrington.of the* Wesleyan
Ex-President.

To-morrow (Sunday) the ex-President of the Wesleyan Conference (Dr Davison) will make his annual visit to Bold-street Church, Warrington. This is the third year in succession that the ex•president has preached the Bold-street anniversary sermons.—The present preacher is second to neither of his distinguished predecessors who have rendered this service to Methodism in Warrington. Dr Davison is professor of theology at Hanclsworth College, Birmingham, and is the author of several valuable and up-tc-lato Biblical works; " The Word in the Heart," notes on the devotional study of Holy Scrip- ture, " The Praises of Israel," " The Wisdom Litfrature of the Old Testament," are amongst the most popular. " The Christian Conscience," the Fernley lecture delivered by Dr Davison before the Conference of 1888 is recognized as an important contribution to Christian ethics. In the forefront of modern scholar- ship, his clear and devout pronouncements upon the findings of the " Higher Criticism" are welcomed by the thoughtful in all the churches as affording safe guidance in disputed matters. The year of Dr Davi- son's presidency, which was cmcluded only last month, was eminently successful ; and the cultured and devout scholar proved himself a wise administrator. In the re- cent Conference at Manchester no voice commanded such immediate and unanimous attention as his, whilst his official deliverances may be taken as models for fol- lowing years.

div.head: Baptist Church, Golborne-street.
div.p: Baptist Church, Golborne-street.

A good congregation assembled on Sunday mornino, when the pastor spoke on the " Garden of Eden " theory of the " Fail." He said he might as well inform them at the outset that he did not accept the story of Genesis as literally true, neither did he think it was ever intended that any one should do so. It ought to be regarded as an attempt made in the childhood of the race to account for what was an existing fact—the presence of sin. The moral reflections put into the lips of Adam and Eve before their fall had not the slightest scriptural authority and although they might perhaps be excused on the score of poetic licence, they were absolutely opposed to scripture and contrary to common sense. It was sometimes asserted that as all good had its source in God, so all evil had its origin in the Devil and that answer was supposed to be a solution to the mystery of evil but he ventured to assert that only a shallow and superficial observer would accept such a solution, to do E 0 would involve them in serious difficulties. So far as he (the preacher) was concerned he was prepared to defend the view that moral evil had its origin in the groi purpose of God. Mr Dunnico then proceeded to discuss the question and in the course of his remarks said,that the origin of evil was likewise the origin of all viTtuq. The •self same power that changed an innocent child co a guilty sinner alone could develope it hereafter into a saint. The moral sense alone made man a sinner and that alone made man a saint. In con- clusion the preacher said that the remedy for sin appeared in the wondrous fact of Redemption,and that the mystery of evil must ever remain to those who re- fused the Christian solution. Great iutereat was shown in and advantage taken of Mr Dunnico's offer to answer any question of interest, from the pulpit. The chapel was crowded at the evening service.

Funeral at Manchester.

Amid manifestations of the deepest, regret the remains of the late Mr William Harris Wright, manager of the Warrington branch of the Manchester Union Bank, who died suddenly at his residence,Hilton House,Paddington, on Thursday of last week, were interred in the Southern Cemetery, Manchester, on Monday. The coffin was taken to Manchester by road, the journey being com- menced at an early hour in the morning, but the mourners left by the 11.27 a m train from Padgate Station•and by the courtesy of the railway company the 3p m express train was stopped at Padgate on the return journey for the convenience of those attending the funeral. The officiating clergy at the cemetery were the Revs W Pollock-Hill, vicar of Padgate, and G Vale- Owen, urate, who Conducted the Service in a very impressivce manner. Amongst those preemie were Mrs W Harris Wright (widow), Mr Heald, Mrs Heald (sister-in-law), Mr Diver and the Misses Heald, (nephew and nieces), Miss May Nield, Mr G Fairhurst (Mouldsworth), Mr John Fairhurst, Mr and Mrs W F Newton, M r and Mrs F Harris, Mr R R Heap (Salford), Dr Bennett (the deceased's medical attendant), Mr Joseph Bennett, jun., Mr Thomas Houghton, Mr James Houghton, Mr William Houghton, Miss Jackson, Mr Percy Royston, Mr and Mrs J Jennings, Mrs William Price and Miss Price, Mr William Grounds, Mr Black- well, Mr Boyd, Mr G Mather, Mr C E Willett, Mr Segar Owen, Mr Gandy (Slanchester Union Bank), Mr Arthur Browne,Mr John Houghton, Mr Thomas Bennett, Mrs Taylor (Chorlton), Miss May War- burton, Miss Houghton, Mr Unwin, Mrs Jackson (nix- ton), Miss Herron, Miss Evans, Mr and Mrs Harrison, Mrs Swire and Mrs Wrigley. Floral tributes were forwarded by the following : Mrs Harris Wright and Master Clarence Harris Wright. Mr and Mrs Heald, Mr Oliver Heald and Miss Jessie Heald, Mr W Houghton and Miss Jackson, Mr and Mrs; D Richardson, Mr and Mrs J H Richardson, Mr and Mrs William Price and family, Mrs William Royston, and family, Mr and Mrs J Jennings, Mr and Mrs , Walter Kerfoot, Mr and Mrs John Fairhurst, Mr and Mrs W F Newton, Mr and Mrs Frank Harris, Mr and Mrs Joseph Bennett, Mr and Mrs Walter Bennett, Dr and Mrs Bennett, Mr and Mrs William Bennett and family, Mr Thomas Bennett and family, Mr Bert Nicholson,Mr and Mrs James Houghton, Mr and Mrs J D Buckton, Mr Thomas Houghton and family Mr and Mrs T Birtles and family, Mr and Mrs Arthur Browne, Mr and Mrs C J Willett, Mr Fowler, Mr Houghton Owens, Mr Gandy, Mr and Mrs Demon and family, the Rev W and Mrs Pollock-Rill, Mrs Philips and Mrs Coward, Mr Connor and family, Mr J t 0 Thomp- son and Miss Thompson, Mr and Mrs Doan (Pendleton), Teachers of Padgate National Sehool, Scholars of Pad- gate National School, Padgate Tennis Club and Arpley Tennis Club. The funeral arrangements were satisfactorily carried out by Mr Edward Connor,of Sankey-street,Warrington, who also supplied the coffin. At Christ Church on Sunday morning, the service was conducted by the Rev J Rogers, curate of Winwick,who made a touching reference to the deceased. The hymns were of a solemn character, and at the conclusion of the service the Dead March in Saul was played by the organist (Mr Blackwell), the congregation remaining standing until it conclasion. In the evening the Rev H I Wadeson, of Croft, officiated, and at the conclusion ef his sermon epoire most feelingly of the good work of the deceased, many members of the congregation being visibly touched. The Dead Mareh was again played.
Presentation to a Lymm Police-Sergeant. _ .

- At Lymm Patty Sessions on Wednesday, the Chairman (Mr Norris), on behalf of the magistrates and residents of the district, presented Sergeant Garner with a purse containing £27 in recognition of services rendered in the district during the past nine years. The Bench, the Clerk, Superintendent Okell, and others enlogised the smart work per formed by Sergeant Garner, who joined the Ches- hire Constabulary sixteen years ago. Sergeant Garner has been transferred to knutsford. and Ser- geant Washington, of Altrincham to Lymm.
