div.p: niE EX.A_IVIINER, FRIDAY, SEPTEMBER 19, 1902.
LIVELY SCENE AT GREAT SAN KEY PARISH COUNCIL MEETING. An Illegal Meeting.

There was a lively scene at the meeting of the Great Sankey Parish Council held on Tuesday evening. I; arose out of the last meeting of the Council, a meeting which the Chairman contended was an illegal one. It will ha remembered that at the time the meeting in question was timed to commence, Mr Thompson was the only member to put in an appearance. After Waiting in vain for some other member to turn up, Mr Thompson adj =nett the meeting and left the room. Shortly after- war is ses,eral members put in an appearance, and Mr Fulton Smith was appointed to take the chair. Business Was transacted in the usual way. The Clerk now asked whether the minutcs of this particular meeting should be read. He had no; recorded them in the minute book. The Chairman (Mr Thompson) : There was no necer- sity for the meeting. I regarded it as illegal. When I got the notice convening the meeting I said at once, without consulting the law books,that it was illegal. But in order to make doubly sure I consulted a solicitor and he confirmed my views that the meeting was illegal. Mr Halton : This matter was discussed at the last meeting, and I don't know why we should be taken advantage of to-nigh; ; as long as a discussicn ensued at the last meeting it was quite sufficient. It is a well- known fact that had we called the Chairman's attention to the fact that we requlred a meeting, and given him a abort notice, we were tulip entitled to call a meeting.

Mr Thompson : Hear. hoar. Mr Hal;cin (continuing) : Therefore Mr Thompson is remiss in calling attention to the matter simply because the reporters are here. It is making capital out of a meeting that was, practically speaking, held for the benefit of the district. Mr Thompson retired because the train was late conveying certain other mernbe•rs to thf- meetine% Do justice to other member, and speakinr, honestly and truly, Mr Thompson must admit, that at every meeting we have attended here we have been punctual with the exception of the meeting in question, and why he should have retired EO early I tail to see. He must have had some intimation. The Chairman : The meeting was called for eight o'clock. I Cams here at eight o'clock and remained ten minutes. Mr Halton : Excuse me ; I give that a total denial. I was her 3 at ten minutes past eight with one or two colleagues—from seven to eight minut2s past eight at any rate. The Chairman : You were not here at ten minutes past eight. Mr II awn : I wan here, and I am telling the truth.

The Chairman. : Ditto. Mr Halton : And you took off, walked out of the room, and went to a hand prietice. Why you did it I should like to have an explanation. The Chairman : I was hero to conduct the meeting. Mr Halton ; I have waited for you on many occasions for ten minutes, and I have not run away as you did. Jr is something extraordinary. The Chairman : I came here to say that the meeting was illegal, and cuild not be legally held. I thought I had waited long enough. Mr Halton : With the advice of whom ? The Chairman : A solicitor. Mr Halton : Independently of the Clerk? The Chairman : Yes, sir. Mr Halton : lam content to take the ruling of the Clerk as long as I am here. The Chairman : If you like I will read the ruling itself. It is the opinion of a solicitor. Mr Halton : I don't think it is necessary to read it. I don't knew what the hubbub is about ; it is taking advantage of our position. The Chairnian : It is a question of the minutes. Mr Halt al Yu are making capital out of the matter, The Chairman : I don't want to make capital out of it. Mr Halton : It is there. The Chairman : lam bete to conduct the business of the meeting, and I will try to do so in a proper manner. What shall we do about the minutes of the meeting that is declared to be illegal ? Mr Halton : Now you are getting to business. The Chairman : I wish you would keep order. Mr Halton : I will keep order if you won't try to make capital out of my colleagues. I The Chairman : It is false. Mr Halton : We place you in power and you should -abide by the ruling. The Chairman : Now gentlemen, let us get to busi- ness. .
It was eventually decided that the correspondence read at the last meeting should be re-read and entered on the minutes of the meating with the decisions thereon.

WHY THE POLICE LEAVE THE DISTRICT. THE ISTRICT TOO LARGE. The Clerk read a copy of a letter he had sent to Police- Sergeant Harris, of Great Sankey, asking him to re-consider his decision to accept a similar position at Darwen. The Sergeant had replied to the effect that he could not re-consider his decision, as he had already removed to Darwen. Toe state of his wife's health would not allow him to remain in the district. Mr Halton thought the health of the sergeant's wife was not the cause of his removal. The district was too large for any one sergeant to overlook. It wai monstrous for the police authorities to expect a man to walk from one end of the district to the other in a day ; it dr3ve a man away. It was high time the Superinten- dent was written to asking him to add Surtonwood to the Earlestown district or give extra help at Sankey and Penketh. (Hear, hear.) The Chtirnaan : I quite agree. The sergeant here has a great deal of work to do. ; Mr Halton: Tbe time has come when extra help ought to be given. THE COST OF THE CORONATION FESTIVITIES. Mr Halton said he was unable to pay the accounts for the Coronation festivities until he received the £36 from the rates. He had received • number of privat3 subscriptions amounting to about £l7. On the motion of Mr Fulton Smith, seconded by Mr Taylor, it was decided that the Coronation Committee be called together, and that a statement of accounts be prepared and audited. and the accounts paid. It was further decided, on the motion of the same gentlemen, that a precept be served on the overseers for £36, and that the Council pay that sum to Mr Halton, hen treasurer to the Coronation Committee, to enable him to settle the accounts. A C HIRSE OF LECTURES TO BE GIVEN. Mr Fulton Smith submitted a letter from Mr Foster, dated, " S.cretary's Office, Penketh," stating that the Winwick Rural Technical Committee at the last meeting decided to pursue the same course as last year, and ask each member to ascertain from his Council meeting what subjects would be most suitable to the district. His committee would then consider what areangements could be made for the holding of classes and lectures in the districts. A. list of the subjects was given. Mr Fulton Smith remarked that the lecturers were well attended last year and were very much appreciated,and the suggestion made seemed to be the best way of taking advantage of the cltsses with regard to secondary edu- cation. His idea was that they Should have another course of lectures, but not necessarily on the same sub- ject—on a subject that would commend itself to the majority of the parishioners. It was decided that Mr Smith arrange for a course of lectures on veterinary science. The subject of instituting classes was referred to the School Board.

MORE GAS LAMPS WANTED. A letter was read from Mr F Taylor, secretary to the Corporation Gas Department, referring to the proposed increase of the lighting accommodation in Sankey dis- trict by the erection of six additional lamps. Mr Taylor minted out that if the additional lamps were provided, the price of the existing lamps would be reduced by 53 per lamp, but it was understood that the new lamps wouldibe erected in the line of route of the existing lamps The Chairman thought an additiond lamp was needed in Hood-lane. Another might be put beyond the Great Sankey schools near Mr Jeans' house. Mr Halton thought Station-road ought to be better lighted. It was pointed out that the existing lamps cost five.

eighflas of a penny in the £. and if eight or nine more lamps were erected the totalcust ta the ratepayers would 'be 1} in the £. On the motion of Mr Fulton Smith, it was decided that the Council approve of the erection of eight or nine additional lamps, the Chairman to see the representa- tives of the Gi Departmsnc with a view to a further reduction in view ot a larger number being ernted.

div.head: LIFEBOAT SATURDAY.
div.p: LIFEBOAT SATURDAY.
Warrington's Effort on behalf of a Worthy Institution.

The people of Warrington will on November Bth be aff irded an opporiuniry of expressing in tangible form their appreciation of the noble work of the Royal Lifeboat Institution That day will be specially sat apart as " Lifeboat Saturday," and a strenuous effort will be made to raise a contribution worthy of the town, to assist in furthering a most deserving cause. The matter was under considera- tion at a meeting held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of Councillor Bennett. There were also present :—Tne Rev W Bracecamp, Messrs Stanley Wilson (deputy town clerk), W H J Jenkins, E Bradshaw, W H Drinkwater, J 11 Smethurst, H Rogers, T Richarilson, and J Reginald Roberts; organizing secretary of the Lifeboat Institution.

The Cna.rumeix read the following letter from the Mayor :—" Staunton Park, Staunton-on-Arrow, Herefordshire, Septeriab.3r 15h, 199. Dear sir,—l much regret tha', being absent from Warrington, I am unable to attend the meeting in support of the Lifeboat Institution in the Town Hall to-morrow. I assure you the movement has my very sincere sym- pathy,and I consider the National Lifeboat Institu- tion one of the noblest and best of our benevolent societies and one which every Englishman should feel bound to support. Hoping you may have a successful meting, I am, yours faithfully, J. CHARLTON PARR, Mayor." Continuing, the Chair- man said it was a curious coincidence that he had just hem spending a little holi- day at Lytham, and the first thing that struck him was the wonderful lifebaat service. At tbe Lifeboat House there was a record of the servic-s rendered by the lifeboat men and the number of lives saved amounted to something like 300. He bad a conversation with the coxswain of the lifeboat, who was said to be the oldest cox- swain in the service, and he told him a great deal which impressed him very much. We were accus- tomed to heroes in this country—in every depart- ment of national life they always seemed to come forward when required—but the unpretentious, modest valour of this plain, blunt man at Lytham impressed him very much.

Air Wilson said the Lifeboat Saturday Fund was founded in Warrington on November sth, 1891 In that year they had a collection. A strong ladies' committee was formed, and boxes were sent round to the various works in the town, with the result that the sum of £295 103 Si was raised, OE that they sent £2OO to the institution, and after paying sundry expenses there was a balance in the bank of £4O ris 4d. In 18,4 another attempt on a small scale was made to raise money, and they sent £5O to the institution. The first effort was most suc- cessful. The town and outlying parishes were on that occasion divided into districts, and each lady took charge of a district and made a house-to-house collection. He was afraid if they had to rely solely upon the collection in the streets it would be small affair, and he would strongly advise them to have a ladies' committee to divide the town and neighbourhood into districts, and to send boxes to every works and to the principal shops in the town. He considered it was quite time Warrington sent a further donation to the Lifeboat Institution, even if it were only .a hundred guineas. _ _

Mr Roberts then delivered an address. At the outset he acknowledged the debt of gratitude which he owed to Mr T El Granger, bon secretary pro tern, for the initial work he had done in connection with the convening of that meeting. Business prevented Mr Granger from being present that evening. The opening of their meeting that night was, from his (the speaker's) point of view, dis- tinctly encouraging. They hal a confirmatory letter from the Mayor reminding them of his sympathy with the movement. Some time age he (Mr RTherts) called on the Mayor and the Mayoress at their residence, and they then expressed their warmest sympathy with the cause. They had in the chair one who had recently been aroused to ieereat in the work, and they had an account of what Warrington did in the early days of Lifeboat Saturday. What Mr Wilson did not say he would like to recall to these present. It was that War- rington was one of the very few towns in the early days of Lifeboat Saturday that spontaneously took up the work ot a town's collection. Pr did rot need any invita- tion from an outsider ence,biat on its own initiation took up the work.Efe remembered that for the size of the town Warrington's collection was one of the most successful that had been made up ta that time, so that they might take it that they had in Warrington a strong feeling of sympathy with that great cause. On the last occasion thrie was just a collection. The programme of a Lifeboat Saturday movement usually included, at any race in its initial stega. a demonstration, when they had the presence of a lifeboat and crew in addition to other attractive Peels such as might be get together locally. One of the things that had cheered him very much in going about Warrington on Monday, and that day had been the'accounts he had heard of the admirable manner in which their hospital movement was organized, realizing such a very hand• some sum. The practical experience taught him that the methods adopted of getting in that large sum of money must have been very complete and exceedingly well carried out. He could only hope that the arrange- ments for a Lifeboat Saturday would be anything like al adequate as the arrangement for the eff on behalf of the hospital. The presence of a lifeboat and crew in an inland town was of the greatest possible interest,and when the launching of the boat could be arranged the interest amounted in many cases to enthusiasm. He did I not knew what the local conveniences were for launch- ing a lifeboat. He had known large sums to be realized when the boat had been launched in apparently very inadequate places. He would not suggest that the boat should be launched unless it could be done in water that ran through private grounds, so that they could make lideharge for witnessing the atteactior. ladies' committee invariably did a good deal of work that ensured the success of the movement. The ladies of Warrington on the last occasion brought about the entire success of the collection, helped by a few gentle- men who were good enough to provide them with what they required in the way of mapping out the districts and supplying boxes, SL'. He would like to make it clear that the collections at the works would be taken only on" nay-day" of Lifeheat Saturday week, and not during a series of weeks. Very often the committees in other towns wound up the day with something of an attractive character, very often an indoor entertain- ment, such as a concert. With regard to the lifeboat movement itself, they would be interested to learn that although they dii not count last year as particularly stormy, neverthelees 00 lives were saved around the Coasts of the United Kingdom. Adding that number to those of previous years. the total number of lives they had to deal with was 43,197 It was difficult to realise

from figures like these what the reality of the work had been, but if one endeavoured to think about the thankfulness that had been felt for the saving of one life that was dear to him—not necessarily from shipwreck but from any danger that threatened—we got a more adequate reali- zation of the grand national work that was heing done by the gallant msn who manned the lifeboats. Life- boat Saturday workers decided some years ago that the money collected by means of these efforts throughout the land should be mid over to the Lifeboat Institution for the specific objects of compensating lifeboat men who were injured whilst doing their perilous work, and the relatives of those who were lost, and also for pro- viding a small retiring pension for men who for a long series of years had been connected with the service. The objeotS, as the Mayor had said, undoubtedly com- mended themselves to every Englishman, and he had no doubt that if they resolved to undertake the work anew in Warrington this year the response of the public would be full and free. There were nearly 300 lifeboats around the coasts of the United Kingdom and they were manned by about 19,000 men. It-was a strictly volun- tary service. It was only the signal calling them to duty that caused them to get into the lifeboats to do their arduous work. It was true they were paid every time they went out for practice and for active service, but the money handed to them for going out could never be regarded as remuneration for the risks which they ran. Those who were responsible for the fund felt that the men willing tc do that work should know that when they got into the lifet o tts thos, who were near and dear to them should be taken care of out of the funds of the Lifeboat Institution should they not return. In con- clusion the speaker said he had no doubt that the people of Warrington would make a generous response to any appeal that was made nn behalf of the institution. It was decided that November Bth should be set apart as" Lifeboat Saturday " in Warrington. An honorary Council, consisting of leading townsmen, was appointed. Mr E Bradshaw was elected hon treasurer and Mr W H Drinkwater loon secretary. A Eclectin,. of ladies for the purpose of forming a com- mittee will be held at an early date.
The officials at the Bing ley Police Court have ceased to administer the oath by kissing the Bible, and have adopted instead the ,Scotch style of swearing with the uplifted hand.
REVISING THE VOTERS' LISTS.
Court at Warrington.

MB. TAYLOR'S CLAIM DISALLOWED. Mr Feard attended on Wednesday for the purpose of signing the lists and •• starring duplicates." Mr Holbrook mentioned the claim of Mr Taylor which the Barrister had adjourned from Monday evening's sitting in order that he might consult authorities on the point raised. The Barrister said he had thoroughly gone into the point and was unable t, allow the claim. Mr Clayton was quite right in his contentions that he (the Barrister) I had no power to alter the claim and make it read that the applicant was a joint user of the sitting-room. The I claim would be disallowed.

At tho close of the proceedings Mr Clayton proposed a vote of thanks to the Revising Barrister. He referred to Mr Foard's courtesy, and said he always exercised great care in all the cases that came before him, and gave claimants every opportunity of maintaining their claims. The list this year was a very good one, and the objections sent in were only 28 per cent, of the num- ber on the list. The list had been very carefully pre- pared by the Assistant Overseers. Mr Holbrook seconded, ar.d commented upon the cor- rectness of the list. The Barrister, in returning thanks, said his duties had been very light, owing to the assistance he had received. Instead of the agents thanking him he ought to thank them for the service they had rendered. He was very pleased they had got through their work so well withou, engendering any bitterness of feeling. Both the agent had their duties to perform and they had done their work in a very creditable manner and with courtesy tot each other .

div.head: GENERAL NEWS
div.p: GENERAL NEWS

An interesting and rather startling confession was made by the Mayor of Southwold at the recent meeting of the Town Council. Referring to his visit to West- minster Abbey for the Coronation ceremony, be said there was a programme and a book on each of the ohair in the area reserved for the Mayors. Two chairs,one on either side of him, were vacant, and be to k possession of the programmes and the books. Later on the gentle- men to whom the seats belonged arrived, and they searched under the chairs and on the floor. He asked them what they were looking for, and on being told, he said, " I can's see them," which was quite true.for they were in his pocket. The Mayor concluded his confession by stating that he would have great pleasure in present- ing a programme to the Corporatime. An attempted " Hooligan" outrage in the Biackfriars road, Southwark,early on Tuesday morning,ended in an amusing mariner, mueh to the disgust of a band of young ruffians. A middle-aged gentleman,formsrly one 1 of the best of English wrestlers, was walking home to Nelson Sgere,when he was suddenly seized from behind by a gang of five, some of whom attempted to rifle his pockets. Toe roughs had, however, reckoned without their host; for quickly collecting himself, their intended victim threw them off, sending two sprawling into the road. Another burley" Hooligan" essayed to cope with the man single-handed,but the victim with a quick movement, " crosied-buttocked " his assailment, who turned a complete somersault and fell heavily on Ws back in the road. The wrestler then dashed at the other roughs, striking cut ri.tht and left, and in a couple of minutes all five were taking to their heels. The New York cerrespondent of the" Yorkshire Post' states that Mrs. Carrie Nation, the Kansas " saloon- = teller," has received an invitation from the Prohibition liance of London to cross the ocean and make war on' ihe public-houses in the British Isles. Mrs. Nation ntende to accept the invitation, and will visit Menthes- tar, Lends, Liverpool, Nottingham, Sheffield, and other Eogliah cities. She says Great Britain is a greater slave to drink than America, and she expects to find no diffi- culty in using her hatchet. Before crossing to England Mrs. Nation intends to found a home in Kansas for the wives and children of drunkards. She is now engaged in selling miniatures of her famous hatchet to pay the fines inflicted on her by unfeeling judges. She is anxious to see President Roosevelt and discuss temperance with him. "The President," she says, "is a beer-drinking Dotehrnan; and lam going to show him the error of bis ways."

There in aro very few firms who have sufficient faith the commodity they produce to send out thousands of samples daily year after year. We can only call one firm to mind, viz., Dr. Tibbles' Vi-Cocoa, Limited, of GO, Bunhill Row, London, E.C., who by this means have introduced the undoubted merits of this wonderful beverage into every home. If any of our readers have not sent for a dainty sample tin they should do so at once.

The Warrington Wesleyan Circuit. The quarterly meeting was held at Lynam on Monday. Tea was provided by the Lymm friends at 530, and their kindness was cordially acknow- ledged by a hearty vote of thanks. After tea the Rev G H Carnson presided over a large gathering. A very hearty welcome was accorded to the chair- man and to thefißev R Wilkins Rees, the new ministers of the circuit.—The Rev G H Carnson, in reply, said Warrington was his first superintend- ency, and he was determined to do his duty at whatever cost. He knew that he would have occasional difficulties, but coolness and op- position would dishearten him. He paid a high' tribute to his colleagues. The Rev RI IWilkins Rees also acknowledged. the welcome.— Mr J W Hayward presented the financial statement which showed t considerable deficit. This was caused mainly by expenses incidental to the recent change of ministers. The membership is exactly as it was last quarter, viz., 893. Mr It Richardson, treasurer to the Worn-out Ministers' Fund, Mr J Barlow, temperance secretary, and Mr Henshall, treasurer of Foreign Mission Fund, were thanked and re-appointed. Half the proceeds of harvest festivals throughout the circuit are to be sent to the circuit stewards towards the circuit deficiency. A proper body of trustees is to be formed for the Bewsey-road Manse. The Rev W C J Neville reported that the whole of the 2.000 guineas promised to the Twentieth Cen- tury Fund had been paid. A strongly worded resolution was passed protesting against the War- rington Circuit being entered in the official lists of the fund as owing 240 guineas more than had ever been promised, and asking for the immediate recti- fication of the misrepresentation—The Chairman announced that the next quarterly meeting would be held at the Bold-street Chapel.

The complete constitution of the Ttoyal Commissiox of Inquiry into the War has now been finally decided on; and, on the whole, the selection must be pronounced very good, containing as it does an ex-Viceroy, an ex-Secretary to the Board of Works, a great Empire builder, a soldier, a sailor, a lawyer, and a contractor, without any personal or political element to bias judgment one way or the other. From this Commission we may hope to get satisfactory results and a reliable report on the questions before it, viz. :—the military preparations for the war in South Africa, and the supplies of men, munitions, equipment, and transport by sea and land, in connection with the campaign, and the military operations up to the occupation of Pretoria, as stated by the Premier on August Bth. As already announced, the Earl of Elgin, who filled the office of Viceroy of India from 1894 to 1899 with considerable distinction, is the chairman; and he will be sup- ported by six representative public men. Viscount Esher is fifty years of age, and sat in Parliament for some years before succeeding to the peerage in 1899. In 1895 he was appointed Secretary to the Board of Works, in which capacity he had a great deal to do with the Coronation prepara- tions; and in July of this year he was made Constable and Deputy-Governor of Windsor Castle. Sir George Taubman-Goldie, P.C., is the founder of Nigeria, and developed that sphere of Imperial influence. He was an officer in the Royal Engineers to start with. Field-Marshal Sir Henry Norman filtered the Indian Army in 1846, and went through the Mutiny. He has held many appointments and had a most distinguished career. He is Governor-General of Chelsea Hospital. Admiral Sir John Ommanney Hopkins, G.C.8., entered the Navy in 1848, and served through the Crimea. He has been Superintendent of Sheerness and Portsmouth Dockyards, Director of Naval Ordnance, Naval Lord ofAhe Admiralty, and has commanded both the North American and Medi- terranean Fleets. Sir John Edge, K.C., was Chief Justice of the North-Western Provinces of India; and Sir John Jackson is one of the largest con- tractors in the world, who amongst other things, carried out the Admiralty who, at Simon's Bay, South Africa. These form a very solid and sensibly- chosen Commission; and their report will be awaited with great interest.

Lieutenant-General Lord William Seymour, who is to succeed Sir William Stirling as Lieutenant of the Tower of London, enjoys the uncommon distinction of having seen active campaigning, both in the Navy and the Army; and his period of service already extends over half a century. The younger son of Admiral Sir George Seymour, G.C.8., G.C.H., he enteted the Navy in 1851, and servaal in the Baltic, being present at the taking of Bomarsuncl. He left the senior service is 1854, and in 1855 joined the Coldstream Guards, with whom he went through the Crimea. In 1861 he went to Canada on the staff, and twenty years later was employed on special duty in Egypt, being present at Mahuta and Tel-el-Kebir amongst oth engagements. Subsequently he went on a special mission to Syria, and from 1883 was employed at headquarters as Acting Military Secretary and Assistant Quar• ter-Master - General. From 1891 to 1896 he was in command LIEUTENANT-GENERAL of the South- LORD WILLIAM SEYMOUR. Eastern District, IHE NEW LIErTESANT or THE and from 1898 TOWER. until 1900 corn-

mended the troops in Canada. He received his courtesy title in 1871, when his brother succeeded to the Marquisate of Hertford, and in the same year married a daughter of the first Lord Penrhyn. Sir William Stirling, whom he succeeds at the Tower, is also a Lieutenant-General, and served in the Royal Artillery from the Crimea onward, rising to be Colonel Commandant. He also saw service in the Indian Mutiny, China (1860), and the Afghan Campaign of 1878-1879. He has been Lieutenant of the Tower since 1900 k and was made 8.C.8. in 1893.

For a short time Ireland has been without a headpiece at Dublin Castle during the interregnum between Lord Cadogan, who resigned his position last July, and his successor, the Earl of Dudley. Next Thursday, however, the new Lord-Lieutenant and his wife enter the Irish capital in State and take up their official residence at Dublin Castle; and their advent is looked forward to with much interest by all sections in the Emerald Isle. No post in the Government is more difficult to fill than the Lord- Lieutenantcy of Ireland, as there are so many absolutely different shades of thought and feeling throughout the country, some of which are of necessity offended when others are pleased and rice versa, and political feeling always runs high. Some of this burden, however, is lifted from Lord Dudley's shoulders by the fact that, unlike his predecessor, he has no seat in the Cabinet, which is now represented in Ireland by Mr. George Wyndham the Chief Secretary. Never- theless, the new Lord-Lieutenant takes up office at a very unpropitious time, and it will take a
TUE NEW LOBD-LIEUTENAITT OF IRELAND AND HIS WI,

MHO ENTER DUBLIN IN SLITS NEXT rntrasn.tv. great deal of ability and tact if he is to make a marked success in a post in which the majority of his predecessors have been conspicuous failures. The Earl of Dudley is a comparatively young man, being only just six-and.thirty ; but for the last seven years he has taken an active part in political life. al

Parliamentary Secretary to the Board of Trade, ant has earnt his promotion by good work. He owns about 30,000 acres of property in Staffordshire and Worcestershire, which contain minerals, and in addition he has large iron works. From these sources and a very large amount of money inherited from his father, the first earl, he is an immensely- wealthy peer and will be able to do the honours of Dublin Castle with a lavish hand,L Lady Dudley, the new hostess of the Castle, wafr one of the well- known Norfolk Gurneys, and N as married just eleven years ago. The Earl and Countess have a son, Lord Ednam, who is heir to the title and the property. All good wishes will go with them next week in this important point in their career.

The Australians will have no cause to feel discontented with the results of the tour which they have just concluded; and it is doubtful whether they have ever sent over a better or more level team. From first to last their success has been most marked, and this is all the more credit- able, as in this wet summer the wickets have been quite different to the "plumb" fast pitches to which they are accustomed in the Antipodes. However, they seemed to settle down to them very quickly; and whilst the conditions made their
(1) J. DARLING, (CAPT.), (2) v. TRUMPER, (3) H. TREMBLE, (4) J. W. SA.IINDEES, (5) M. A. NOBLE.
THE AIISTRALIAN CRICKETERS' WHO HAVE EIS-
TINGUISHED THEMSELVES MOST.

bowling the more deadly, they did not seem to detract from their batting abilities, as they certainly have done in the case of certain prominent English cricketers. In fact, never have so many Australians scored their thousand runs on a previous tour, while Victor Trumper has created a great personal record in being the first Colonial to cross the " rubicon. This he has done very handsomely with, an average of practically 50 per innings, and a. record number of centuries. In fact, he has been the great success of the tour; and the Australians, who claim that he is the finest batsman the world. has ever seen, are, perhaps with one or two. exceptons, not so far wide of the mark. He is certainly a most brilliant exponent of the game and a grand man to send in first. Darling has exercised his usual skill as a captain, but has not had a very successful season personally, though he has made more than a thousand runs. Next to Trumper, Noble has been the most consistent with the bat and has done exceptionally well under the trying conditions. Trumble comes out first with the ball with a splendid analysis, while Saunders, whose action has proved very puzzling, has also taken over a hundred wickets at a comparatively low cost. The rest of the team have all done well; and it is their combined consistency which has made them so bad to beat. They go on to South Africa, where they will play five matches on their way home : and, with their great record and the test match" rubber won, they may leave England extremely well pleased with themselves, in con- clusion, it may be noted with regret that Darling, Trumble, Gregory, Howell and Jones will not come over again—in an active capacity at any rate.

Probably no dog without pretensions to pedigree, and few with, have ever been so well known as "Tim," of Paddington, the half-bred Airedale and Irish terrier, who for so many years collected money on the station for the Widows' and Orphans' Fund. ill connection with the Great Western Railway. This old philanthropist for fourteen years has
THE EARL AND COUNTESS OF DUDLEY,
" TIM," TIIE TERRIER,
WHO COLLECTLD MONEY AT PADDINGTON STITIOi FOR

div.head: FOURTIsIiN YEAILS,
div.p: FOURTIsIiN YEAILS,

trotted all over the great station with a money-box round his neck, and was almost human enough to beg actively for his good Cause. Anyhow it was always said at Paddington that he had sagacity enough to know when a royal train was expected, and always to be right on the spot on those auspicious occasions. However, whether " Tim " knew royalty or not, they errtainly knew him ; an& the late Queen often sent for the old, dog, who was a great favourite of hers, to slip a sovereign into his tin. King Edward, too, has been a constant patron of the importunate, yet popular "Tim." He was the property of Inspector bush, who out of curi- osity, always kept a special account book recording " Tim's " takings; and this shows his daily average to have been four-and-sixpence, and his sum total for fourteen years' unremitting work just on a thousand pounds! Now he has passed away, full of days and loved and respected by all who knew him; but his work will live after him, as old " Tim " is to be stuffed and placed on the station to carry on passively the work in which he was se active in his life-time. Many will stop and subscribe as they pastahe old stuffed dog, and remember him, with regret. His life was well spent; and old "Tim" won for himself fame that was almost world-wide. •

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.

porating them in France. But Lord MILER is more despotic than NAPOLEON. Or take, again, the language question. The Generals demand equality for the Dutch and English languages in the schools and the law courts. That is the rule in Cape Colony, and the French Canadians enjoy a similar privilege. We encourage Gaelic and Welsh, and even Irish at home. Why attempt to suppress the Dutch ? We have ignominiously failed to impose English by force on the Maltese. It is folly to prepare for ourselves the cup of diffi- culties with which the Prussians are struggling in German Poland. Finally there is the question k,f amnesty for the rebels. Lord KITCFIENER favours a generous policy. Is it quite certain that Lord MILNER, is the wiser man of the two ?
BUT the real difficulty
A Ruined Race. is an economic ques-

tion. The Boers are a ruined race, in a financial sense. There are few of them who have not lost in the devastations of the past two years, farmstead and furniture, implements and live-stock. They have nothing left but their naked hands. To Lord MILNER this seems a glorious opportunity. He proposes to utilise their distress in order to buy land whole- sale, if necessary, by compulsory powers, in order to settle British farmers upon it. But, you will say we are granting the Boers £3,000,000 :to re-stock and re-build their farms. How far wiil that go ? It would amount, if evenly distributed, to about k6O a head. As a waggon and a team:of oxen cost £2OO, that will not go far. And will it be evenly distributed P In the first place it is to go not to each according to his need, but to those who hold receipts for goods commandeered by the Republics during the war, and naturally those who lost most had the least to com- mandeer. In the second place, the com- missions which distribute the money consist largely of National Scouts—renegade Boers who are rightly despised by their countrymen. In short, the future seems gloomy in the extreme, and thousands of men who before the war . were prosperous yeomen, owning and farming their own land, look forward to the hard fate of becom- ing sewers of wood and drawers of water. A more impolitic course we could hardly pursue. A proud man may be forced to acquiescence in. the loss of his country's independence, but he will fight hard before he accepts a position of personal subjection. It is worse than impolitic, however : it is unjust. These men lost their all, because we chose to do the recognized laws of- war which protect the pro- perty of individual belligerents. We burnt their farms, in hundreds of cases, simply because the owner was, in the official phrase, "absent on com- mando." Ho has an absolute right to demand compensation. Nor is General BOTHA unreason- able in asking us to do something for the widows and orphans of the men who fell. We have in- herited the duties of the Republics which we destroyed. We have taken over their assets, their gold-fields, and their crown-lands. We cannot repudiate their obligations.

If perseverance were always fittingly rewarded Mr;11 A Naylor would soon be free from the no- torious Thelwall nuisance,but even in a just world men do not invariably get their deserts. We could not say, from memory, how long Mr Naylor has been waging war against the horrible stench which so frequently one lopes his home at Thelwall ; the commencement of the strife is shrouded in the obscurity of a distant past, but , , the struggle—like the stench—still continues, and people sicken and die, if not like flies in autumn at any rate with alarming frequency. Yet the Runcorn Rural District Council does nothing but display the most culpable ineptitude and almost criminal indifference. Mr Naylor does well ' to bombard them with Dr Penny's re- port, for which they paid 65 guineas, and then relegated it to the limbo of obscurity. We know of no instance in local government which reflects so gravely upon the administration of a local authority. Whether they are aware or not of the real cause of the nuisance, the Rural Council are guilty of a dereliction of public duty which ought to havellong ago called upon them the vengeance of the supreme authority. Mr. Naylor has our full sympathy in this matter, and we hope he will ultimately succeed in getting the Thelwall nuisance " at whatever cost to the Council or individuals. 'MS _ .

We commend to British Protectionists a care- ful study of the condition into which Protection has brought Germany in the matter of food. The Prussian Chamber of Agriculture has published a report which shews that even the farmers and millers are suffering from the exclusion of foreign grain by high tariffs, while meat, especially the cheaper kinds of meat, such as pork, which, in the shape of sausages, form a large por- tion of the food of the poorer classes, has reached so high a price Ihat it has almost disappeared from the market. Wages have fallen, and the price of meat has risen 20 per cent., and of nearly every other necessary in similar proportions. As there is no scarcity in other countries, the cause can only be found in the prohibitive tariffs imposed on these articles to please the agrarian Protec- tionists. If the working classes in this country would send a deputation of their members t.,) Germany, they would learn a lesson which would save them and their children from the danger to which under the present Tory Government they are exposed.

It is stated in an American magazine that interest in athletics is increasing among American girls. We are given photographs of them perform- ing high jumps, long jumps, engaging in obstacle races—in short, doing most of the athletic exer- cises which formerly appertained to schoolboys only. We cannot pretend that these displays are graceful. But the sama might be said of learning to dance, of the training in deportment which is undertaken for the stage, and of a score or more other exercises preliminary to some achievement. The question is, What is the ultimate result ? The advocates of athletic exercises aver that girls who have the courage to undertake these feats become healthier, more supple of figure, and secure a better carriage. As a matter of fact, the American girl doss not want more carriage: she would appear more beautiful if she had less. The type is a little too pert—a kind of note of exclamation; when in England, at any rate, she seems, as artists say, "out of the picture." But the bearing of English women is for the most part worse in its neglect of any sense of dignity; and those who o wish to appear dignified generally strut. The majority, after reaching thirty years f age, drag themselves along in a slovenly manner. Sprightli- ness seems to be a mere passing phrase of youth. In their horror of French smartness, they forget that there is a happy medium, and that the Viennese, at least, attain it with some distinction. If athletic exercises will lengthen the time of gracefulness and give to grown-up women those maiden movements, "light and free," which excited the admiration of so sedate a sentimental- , ist as Wordsworth, they should be earnestly cultivated. But it should be clearly understood they are not to be followed by innovations in dress —the divided skirt, knickerbockers,or other feeble pretensions to man's inheritance As to health, much depends on the physical and early up- bringing. Girls tenderly reared should hold their ambition in careful restraint. ,

Fortunately the inauguration of the electric tramway system in Warrington has not brought in its train any of those frightful tramcar acci- dents from which other towns have suffered. The recent accident in Glasgow has produced a shock

div.head: SEP rum BICH 19th 1902
div.p: SEP rum BICH 19th 1902

Ttin encounter of the Shylock as three Boer Generals with Statesman. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, which is now recorded in an official publication, will not, we fancy, be a chapter on which students of BritiO history will linger very affactionately in the future. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN doubtless scored a cheap triumph. It is easy to triumph over defeated soldiers, especially when they happen to

be—as Generals .BDT-11A., DE WET, and DELAREY clearly are—simple men of action,more at home in the saddle than in the CJuncil room. Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN, to be sure, was perfectly courteous. "What he did was simply to insist on the hard letter of the treaty of Vereeniging. As the " Manches- ter Guardian" very neatly put it, he adopted the attitude of Shylock, and to each fresh request or suggestion from the Boers he, merely replied : "I cannot find it ; 'tis not in the bond." It is quite true that the Beers did prefer a number of requests for more generous treatment than we allowed in the instrument which ended the war. Bat was that really a matter for indignation or surprise? The treaty was not a settlement dictat- ed either by abstract justice or disinterested generosity. It may have been fair enough as such treaties go. But we granted simply the minimum which we calculated the alers in their hard plight would accept. Oar aim was to end the war, and we allowed just as much as was necessary to achieve that object. There was little or no discussion. We simply dictated an ultimatum by superior force. Had we been in a position to finish the war quickly
we should have granted less; had the Boers been less exhausted,or less appalled by the sufferings of their women and child ren,we should probably have grant-

ed more. But all that is over, and our object is now not so much to complete a conquest as to make the conquered territory as m@derately con- tented as the circumstances will allow. Surely to men who meet as with frank professions of loyalty we may concede more than we were willing to grant when they sat round a table with arms in their hands and their commandos in the back- ground? We are dealing now not with enemies, but with fellow-subjects. Perhaps the Boers put some of their demands in a rather startling form ;

they are not diplomatists, but veterans. Take for ex trnple their most extreme demand. They ought not to have asked for the reinstatement or com- pensation of their old officials as a matter of right. But we might very well have answered that where an official had a good record, was generally respected and loyb.lly accepted the new regime, we would do our .best to find him employment. That would have been fair and wise. Mr. CHAMBER- , LAIN, however, simply refused to discuss the ques- tion. That attitude may win a little cheap applause in London, but it certainly will not smooth out the tangles in South Africa. _
THE grievances which the

Boer Generals wished to discuss were for the most part decidedly real. General BornA,whose farm is in the Vryheid district, complained bitterly that this large territory had been detached from the Transvaal, and handed bodily to Natal. The attitude of Natal, he complained is bitterly hostile to the Boers,and he is so sure that,as a minority,they will not meet with fair treatment that he and his neighbours are about to emigrate elsewhere in a body. Is this what we desire? The grievance is a real one, for the President of the Outlander Refugee Committee, Mr. SHEPPERD, who is assur- edly no Pro-Boer, strongly backs the GENERAL'S statement in a letter to the"lVlorning Leader." The transfer was an autocratic act of Lord MILNER'S. He consulted no one on the spot, Parliament has had [no say in the matter, and now General BOTHA is told that the thing is irrevocable, and simply cannot be discussed. When NAPOLEQN 11. annexed Savoy with the consent of Italy, he ook a plebiscite of the inhabitants before incor.
Real Grievances.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDA V SEPTEMBER 19. 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDA V SEPTEMBER 19. 1902

throughout the country and is well calculated to make nervous people chary at using the electric cars. At Glasgow the tramcar became unmanage- able owing to the brake ratchet handle coming away in the motorman's hand in consequence of the locker pin having worked loose andicoine out. The result was that the car backed downhill and collided with a car standing on the up-rails and the two ultimately crashed into a third. The three cars moved back and left the rails at the points. A lady passenger was killed, and nearly thirty othbr persons were injured. Such a calamity 'as this should cause tramway committees and managers throughout the country to see that the cars are fully equipped to meet cases of emerg- ency. An additional brake in this instance might have prevented the accident. At Oldham where there are many steep gradients, the authorities have had an emergency brake fitted to each car, and this brake acts on the rails instead of the wheels. Since its adoption Oldham has been free from accidents. There are no gradients in War- rington similar to those in Oldham or Glasgow,but we hope the lesson taught by the recent accident will not be lost on our local tramways committee.

There was an interesting discussion at the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guar- dians on Wednesday last week on the merits and demerits of paying for new buildings and exten- sions out of current revenue instead of resorting to the usual custom of raising a loan. The Clerk has found it necessary to ask for an additional penny to be added to the poor rate for the impend• ing half-year, making the rate sevenpence instead of sixpence in the pound. This increased call is largely due to the erection of new relief offices at Earlestown, the cost of which it is proposed to pay out of the current year's revenue. Other poor law authorities would not have had the least com- punction in raising a loan for the amount required and repaying it by easy instalments of principal and interest in a term of years. But the Warring- ton Board, largely influenced by the advice of the [ Clerk, has steadfastly refused to incur loans for such purposes, and the result of this economic policy is that the whole of the outstanding debts of the Union are so small that a rate of is. fid. in the £ would suffice to extinguish them.

div.head: ST. HELENS TRADE WAR. ---- "Stores " and the "Boycott."
div.p: ST. HELENS TRADE WAR. ---- "Stores " and the "Boycott."
Interesting Statement.

The " trade war " at Sr. Helens between the St. Helens and District Traders' Defence Association on the one hand and the St. Helens Industrial Co-operative Society on the other continues to excite attention in many parts of the country. The movement on the part of the Br. Helens tradesm:n, to exercise every legitimate means of influencing the townspeople against tee Co- operative Society, was initiated a couple of months age and, in view of these efforts and action on the part of the Traders' Defence A.ssociation, an official statement from the Co-operative Society has been anxiously awaited. This has just been issue I, and the statistics given form very interesting reading in view of the expected disastrous effect upon the operations of the society of the united action of the tralespeople. It will be remembered that the Traders' Defence Association recommended that members of that body— which comprises practically all the private tradesmen in the town—should decline to bank money with banks whose managers were connected with the society ; that support should be withdrawn from ministers of churches or chapels who favoured the c)-operative movement ; that tradesmen generally should support each other in every possible way, and refuse to employ the eons or daughters of anyone dealing at the co-operative stores. That the tradesmen of St Helens have actively bestirred themselves in the directions indicated is well knowa,and the spread of the anti-co-operative movement to other parts of the country, together with the interest which has been aroused among all classes, is sufficient testi- mony to the eacrgy which the St Hslens Traders' De- fence Association has thrown into the campaign. It has been a most remarkable circumstance that throughout the wills of the op-rations hitherto the officials and managers of the St Helens Co-operative Society have maintained a strict reticence. Visits to the offices of the society, interviews with the manager; and officials, have always, without exception, elicited the simple reply," We have no information of any kind to give," and, apparently, the society, which has made almost phenomenal progress since its institution about 17 years agn,was treating the attack upoa it and its busi- ness without concern or alarm in any way. It was, how- ever, hoped by the private traders and their friends that the quarterly statement of the society.issupd to members would bear some indication of the action of the Traders' Defence Association in a greatly reduced membership, and, possibly,a marked decrease in the "sales" amount. It should be remembered, however, that the society's quarter ended ou the 2nd lust, and the Traders' Defence Association was only formel a couple of months ago, so that the effect of the traders' movements may be more conspicuous in the future than in the quarter just con- cluded. However, the St Helens Industrial Co-operative Society have just issued a statement in regard to the last quarter, which in view of the traders' action,excites some attention. The statement, it will be noticed, thoroughly conforms to the " policy of silence " on the part of the officials to the greitly-discussed "trade war." It is as follows : " St. Helens Industrial Co-operative Society, Limited. —To the Members,—We have much pleasure in stating that the sales of the society for the quarter ending Sep- tember 2nd, show an increase of £5,553 13s 41i as com- pared with the corresponding period eat last year. The figures are as follows . s. d. 1902, June to September (13 weeks) 59 940 13 7i 1901, ditto (13 weeks) 54,357 0 3

This statement is signed "Foe the committee, J M Glen, secretary," and is t)e first public announcement by the society since the initiation of the attack upon its operations. The stat sment would seem to indicate that the society'a progress has been practically uninterrupted during the past quarter, at all events, but when com- pared more fully with previous reports there is some in- dication—From the traders' point of view—ht the past quarter has not been quite so " progressive " for the sores as the foregoing statement would seem to prove. As an instance it may he stated that the sales for the past quarter were £59,940 13s 70. an increase of £5,583 134 ni over the correspo )(ling period lsst year. But the society's report for the quarter ending June 3rd last shows that the " sales" amounted to £64,708 93 10J, an increase of £6021 1s id over those for the corresponding period in 1901. I Thus, for the June quarter the " sales " were £64,708 91 103, while according to the society's statement the " sales " for the quarter just concluded were only £59,940 13s 71d, or a decrease of £4,781 16s 21d. It is interesting C 9 note that the decrease in the correspond- ing quarters last year was only £3,320 83 6d. Again,the ' numner of those who joined the society during the I quarter jest concluded was 364, while during the previ- ous quarter the new numbers totalled 400. div.head: LABOUR REPRESENTATION. Formation of an Election Committee. at Warrington.
div.p: LABOUR REPRESENTATION. Formation of an Election Committee. at Warrington.

Another conference in contention vii;t!i the I ehour representatioa movement was L1:li in the Druids' Hall, Warrington,on Tuesday evening, Mr F Stott (secretary of the Trades and L tbour Council) pr !siding. Dele- gates representing seventeen trades union branches, the trades Council and t c Independent Labour Party were present. A re ioluriou was unanimously carried defini- tely deciding t ) form an E ection Cemmittee to be ' called the Warrington Labour Represeetation Csairnittee for the purpose of securing direct and independent repre- senl a don of the inclustri d classes on all local governing bodies and in the House of Commons. Mr C F Eaton (Bakers) was elected secretary(pro tern) of the committee. , In addressing the delegate, the CRAIRMIN said that now it had been definitely decided to form a committee it would be very necessary before taking part in any elections to educate the working classes to the point of desiring tol have direct labour representation. The committee could not do mu An without the support of the electors. They must be prepared to pay not only I the election expenses of candidates, but also for loss of wages which might be incurred by candidates who were successful in being returned to the Town Council or Board of Guardians. Another matter which he do dred to mention, and which was, in his opinion, the most imnortant,was that the committee must keep on stric.ly independent lines. Let them be prepared to co-operate with any genuine labour organizations, but to steer clear of any political alliances. Past history proved to them that they could hope for nothing from either Liberal or Conservative parties which would be of much benefit to tne working classes. They had had promises in abund- ance, and they were yet unfulfilled. The various work- ing class organizations would be approached, especially by the Liberal Party,who would offer all kinds of induce- ments with the la spa of gettiag into power again. Let them (the workers) recognise that if they began to f irm alliances with either of them their (the workers') down- fall would come. Let them stand firm for independence. Let them be united, net only in the trades union branches, but also at the ballot box, and then their efforts would be crowned with success. A code of rules was discussed and derided upon. It was also decided to hold the next meetin in October for the purpose of electing officers, &e, and for making arrangements for carrying oct the objects of the committee.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO A METHODIST VETERAN.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO A METHODIST VETERAN.

The Brunswick Mutual Improvement Class opened its 41st year ou Wednesday under the Presidency of Mr A Wells with a social and musical eveniog. The principal item was the presentation of a gold watch to its late president Mr T Simister who had locen the head of the Society for more than 40 years. Several eulogistic speeches were given by the past and present members of the class. Mr. F. J. Norman J.P., as an old member paid a high tribute to the worth of the retiring president. Metiood- ism, he said, made men, and Mr Simister was one of her choicest fruits. The good he had done in his position was much too vast to be estimated. As be thought of his work which must be one of his finest trophies and of past recollection in which many brilliant men had a place, he felt touched with an emotion keener than ever he had done before. The younger members of the society had all their work cut out if they were to emul- ate the past history of the s3ciey. Be prayed that the eventide of Mr Simister's life would be one of peace and quietness arid that the class would continue to be as eticcesful under is new president as under its late honoured one. Mr Blshrown, the oldest member of the class, then presented the watch amid the applause of those present. They all regretted the step Mr Simister had been forced t I take. His earliest recollect on of Mr Simister were of the most kindly description. Re was a tower tf strength to Runcorn Methodists, and they were extremely sorry to lose his valuable aid. Mr Simister, in response, epraking under deep emotion, said be thanked them for the honour done to him. He was quite unaware until he got into the room that he occupied any portion in the programme. He did not know how to express himself fcr the love shown to him. Re would always prize the watch. Be never expected to possess a gold watch. The welfare of the Society had always been near his heatt. It helped the young meta to he intellectual, and the intellectual men were what the Churo wanted. He hoped the future of the class would he a most prosperous one. The meeting was subsequently brought to a close by a short prayer by the Superintendent Minister, the Rev Alfred Wells.

The programme for the 22ad inst is " Publiu House Trusts and Liquor Municipalisa• tion," a paper issued by 13ro Runs, Grand k.:iyief Templar of hngland. PRIM PUBLIC LIBRAILY.

The monthly meeting of the above committee was held o.)n Tuesday when the following report of the librarian, Mr Jones, was submitted and approved. Number of days open 20, number of issues 1,889 daily average 94, an increase of 39 in the reference department and 149 in the lending department, compared with the corresponding month of last year. The number of issues in each eapartment was as follows : Theology 31, philosophy 10, science 74, history, EL.% 75, poetry 9, fiction 1,441, miscellaneous 168, French literature 3, and music 3. There were 75 issues from the reference depart- ment. This was all the business of general interest THE EDUCATION BILL, RUNCORN FREE CHURCH COUNCIL, AND THE PAYMENT OF THE RATES. At a meeting of the Runcorn Free Church Council held in St John's Schoolroom, on Friday. evening. Mr J Pritchard, president, in the chair, the follow- ing resolution was passed; We urge a strenuous opposition to the passing of the Education Bill, and as a last resort are prepaie 1 to enrol the names and addresses of those who feel they are bound to refuse payment of the rates levied under this Bill should it become law." A copy of the resolution has been sent to the National Council. The Run- corn Council inteud to commence a campaign against the Bill immediately. Toe details have been left to be settled by the Executive Committee. RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE. An interesting meeting of the membrs of the Runcorn Branch of the Order of the Sons of 'uem- perance was held on Saturday night in the Green- way-road School. Mr Thomas R Whyte presided. After the routine business had been transacted, a number of short addresses were delivered. The various speakers referred with much satisfaction to the recent demonstration. Ia every respect it had been a s.uccess,aud had been the means of push- ing forward their propaganda of total abstinence from all intoxicating liquors. It was felt that a forward movement had bee,u made, and that it would lead to a large accession of members both to the adult and the juvenile sections. Satisfaction I was expressed at the way the speakers and Ipreachers had been received at the various places of worship, the Sunday schools and at the P.S.A. at Bethesda. The following officers took part in the meeting: Messrs Daniel Bisbrown, Edward Key, George Powell, James Johnson, Joseph Walker, Thomas J Holt and the President. RUNCORN FOOTBALLERS UNPLEASANT ExpERIENcE The Runcorn football team and officials travelled from Bradford on Saturday night in a special saloon carriage, and at Huddersfield the carriage was uncoupled from the train to be attached to the Newcastle and Liverpool train. An engine was being brought up to take the carriage to the Liver- pool line, when turougn some cause or another the brake refused to act and the engine crashed into the carriage, sending it far up the line. The foot- ball party were violently thrown from their seats by the collision, and for a moment or two the great- est confusion prevailed. It. was then found that with the exception of Lightfoot, who hurt one of his fingers rather badly, no one was injured, though as may be imagined, all the party were severely shaken, and very much alarmed. The front part of the carriage was smashed, and the engine was also damaged, A breakdown gang repaired the damage, and the saloon carriage was attached to the Liverpool train and the party proceeded with their journey. A railway man had a very narrow escape from death. He was waiting to couple the carriage to the engine, and perceiving that some- thing was wrong managed to jump out of the way jest in time. Dia footballers are to be congratu-
lsted upon their fortunate escape. The force of the collision was such that had any other carriages been attached to the saloon carriage it would inevit- ably have been wrecked.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT]

The Runzorn Free Church Council in common with the majority of such Councils have decided upon active resistaece to the Education Bill. They are tol be commended for their attitude. 1 believe the clause respecting the plebiscite to be taken in the event of the Bill passing in order to determine how many of the inhabitants would refuse to pay the hateful rate,was not passed without a very hot discussion. It is to be hoped that when the time comes Nonconformists will be too ad sturdy enough to make a sacrifice and stanl firm in defence of their principles,
The Rev Osborne is no longer secretary to the Free Courch Council His resignation has been accepted though it has not yet transpired who is to fill the vacant post.

[BY ANOTHER CORRESPONDENT ] Mr Simister, for forty years president of the Brunswick alutual,on Wednesday definitely severed his connection with the society, whose fortunes he has so ably safeguarded for so long a period. His resignation has caused widespread regret among all the past and present members of his clasa. Mr Simister can truly be termed a strong man. He has essentially been the architect of his own destiny. At an early age he was, practically speaking,thrown upon his own resources, but being a pronounced believer in " hard work," and wrapt in a religion which made the weightiest difficulties seem light, he successfully negotiated all obstacles until at the present ,moment he unquestionably occupies the foremost position in the nearts of all Runcorn Methodists. Perhaps no man was more 11 fitted than Mr Simister to control the destinies of an intellectual organization such as the Brunswick Mutual Improvement Society. Being naturally of an inquiring mind the different subjects broached at the weekly meetings were carefully studied be- forehand so that he could be in sympathy with the essayist of the evening. Some of the foremost men in the different branches of thought have been con- nected at one time or another with the society,and been sensibly influenced for good. Though Mr Sinister leaves the society his influence will remain. He carries with him into his partial retirement the deep respect, the good wishes, the enduring love of all with whom he has come in contact, and the fervent prayer of all must be that in the eventide of hi life, the light of God's grace willlshine for him clearer and clearer until he enters upon God's eternal day.

Some little senss7io-n— Tia-6:-caused oa Sunday evening at the Salvation Army Barracks, Academy- street, shortly after the commencement of the service. The usual weekly meetinas of the " Young Mission "Juvenile Temple, and the "Temperance Mission",lodge of the 10 G T,were held on Wednes- day evening in the Ebenezer l'tfission Roorn,Butter- market-street. At the junior meeting 'Sister Fry, C T, presided, and eight new members were pro- posed. An encouraging address was delivered by Bro Merlin of the adult lodge. Recitations were rendered by sisters F Littlewo)d,U Broughton,Pry, Lawless, and Bro W Ellis. A vote of thanks was passed to Bro Egerton for framing the charter. The members of the adult lodge were favoured with a visit from the "Excelsior " lodge, Ashton. A fair number of the public also attended. Bro Merlin,

T, opened the lodge, and two new members were ,nitiated. After the usual business, Bro O'Brien related a few reminiscences of his vists to lodges in Lancaster, Carlisle, and Penrith. Bra Nurse sang a solo. The meeting was then taken charge of by the visitors. Bro Vint took the chair and gave a brief address' congratulating the members or. the success of the lodge since the re-opening and urging t'em to continue their efforts to stem the tide of the drink traffic. Sister Vint also spoke and related, some interesting incidents in her life as a Go3d Templar. A short musical programme was then given and refreshments were handed round. Bro Roberts proposed a vote of thanks to the visitors for their presence. Bro O'Brien seconded, Bro Drury supported and the motion was carried with what the chairman termed as " a good old Lanca- shire clap." Bro Vint replie I and a very pleasant meeting came to a close.

. The exhibition which was opened in the St. James's Hall, Mancuester, last wesk is both valu- able and interesting The exhibits are numerous, 1 and their variety is a perpetual surprise to the ' chance visitor. The exhibition is divided into the four following divisions:—(a) Science.in relation to hygiene ; (b) hygiene of special classes, trades and professions, such as schools, hospitals, fire preven- tion &c.; (c) construction and sanitary apparatus', including building materials, water supply, and sewerage, heating, lighting, and ventilation ; d) personal and domestic hygiene. Mot of the principal manufactnrers in the country are represented. The ingenuity of the appliances which crowd every stall are good evi- dence of the skill and intelligence now being given to the improvement of sanitation. There are many exhibits which cannot :be included under any of the above four heads. We are not aware that there is anything especially sanitary about typewriters and jewellery, or that c,-uifectionsry has important hygienic properties. Other exhibi; s, such as wash- ing machines and knife cleaners have no doub', right to a place. if " domestic hygiene" is gener- ously interpreted. But it cannot be said that the main purpose of the exhibition is lost sight of, so niimerous and excellent are the appliances relating to drainage, refuse disposal, ventilation, and dis- infection. The plumbers of Manchester and district will give exhibitions of their skill during the time the exhibition remains open. The general public is attracted to the exhibition by means of band per- formances and demonstration of various kinds. Thus

it may happen that a citizen who came to the exhibition bent on agreeable diversion may leave it seriously impressed by the wonders of sanitary science.—Further particulars of the attractions at the exhibition may be gleaned from our advertising columns.

At the Warrington Connll7(Pitt-t-iSessions on Wednesday, before Messrs F A Frost (presiding) nod 3 Ball, two boys named William Francis and Charles Bebbington, residing in Plerpoint-street, ware summoned for placing two wooden keys and an Iron holt on the Cheshire Lines Railway at Sankey on September list with intent to endanger the eafetv of passengers. They pleaded guilty. Mr Lingard, solicitor, Manchester. prosecuted on behalf of the Cheshire Lines Committee.—George Monks, a platelayer, residing at 55, Gorfsey-lane. stated that on the date named he was travelling by the 2.5 p.m. train from Warrington to Liverpool. Toe train was approaching Sankey when he received Information that there was an obstruction on the line about threequarters of a mile ahead. The train was stopped and witness pre. (seeded to the spot on a light engine. He found two wooden keys and an iron b3it placed across one of the metals. The boys were looking over an adjacent bridge, and witness went along the road and met them. He cauyht Francis, who laid the blame upon Bebbington.—Joseph Jones, a constable in the employ ot the Cheshire Lines Com- mittee, said he received Francis into custody, and the lad at first gave him a wrong arldress.—A detective employed by I the committee said he charged the boys with the offence and they blamed one another. Some other boys who witnessed the affair said Francis placed the obstruction on the line.— Francis now stated that he put the bolt on the line and Bebbington placed the keys there.—The magistrates ordered the boys to receive six. strokes each with the birch rod the Chairman remarking that if an express had ran over the obstruction, the train would probably have been wrecked. SAVAGE ASSAULT ON A FATHER AT WARRINGTON. At the Warrington Police Court on Wednesday, before Alderman Hutchinson and Mr J It Young, John O'Malley. 8, Dolman's-lane, was charged with having been an absentee from the Lancashire Garrison Artillery Militia, stationed at Seatorth, since June 9. Ile was also charged with aesaulting his father, John O'Malley and Richard Aylward in Dolman's- lane on Tuesday night.—P C Cooper said he was on duty in Bridge-street at nine o'clock on Tuesday night when he was informed that a disturbance was going on in Dolman's-lane. He went there and found the prisoner who was partially stripped. His father was bleeding very much from his heft and Aylward had also been assaulted. The prisoner was in a very excited condition and threatened to assault his father In witness's presence. A heavy stick which was covered with blood was found near the prisoner. Both of the injured men were conveyed to the Infirmary where their injuries were dressed. In the circumstances he considered it better to arrest the prisoner, who turned out to be an absentee as his name was found in thtt " Gazette."- -P:isoner's father, whose head was swathed in bandages, stated that Aylward, who VIM a journeyman tailor, called to see him on Tuesday and they had a think or two together. Prisoner became most violent and knocked Aylward down. Witness interfered to prevent any further trouble, and prisoner turned upon him and struck him on the head with something hard. What the bow was dealt with he could not say, but It was not with the stick.--Aylward said the prisoner got excited and began " lashing about " with the stick. He struck witness on the bead with it, and also struck hl a father —Prisoner said he pushed his father who fell down and the injuries were due to the fall.—Prisoner was commit- ted to goal for seven days for each assault, and after this time has expired he will be handed over to a military escort. warrington County Petty Sessions.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
MARGARET ()AXES ATTEMPTS SUICIDE-" WANTED TO DO
THE STATE SOME SERVICE. " - -

At the-WarringTo—n--Police Court on Friday. before the Deputy-Mayor and other magistrates Margaret Oakes,a well- known character, was charged with attempting to commit suicide by drowning herself in the Mersey at two o'clock that morning.—The Chief Constable said he should ask the magistrates to remand prisoner in custody for a week in order that her state of mind might be inquired into. She was as well known to most of the members of the Bench as she was to himself (Mr Talbot). One magistrate tried his best:with effort and with money to do something for her. but she would not he helped and had to be protected against herself. On Thursday night she seemed to have taken a new departure,and seeming almost prompted to do the State some service, attempted to commit suicide. At ',two o'clock that morning a boatman named Thomas Edwards heard some screaming and went to Bishop's Wharf. Prisoner was standing there shouting "Do let me jump in" althongh no one was restraining her. She was prevented from jumping in and taken to the Police Station. She made a statement to the Bridewell officer to the effect that she had had some tronble at home, and they had been so unreasonable as to ask her to get work. (Laughter.) She therefore thought she would be better dead.—Prisoner, on being asked if she had anything to say. said she would be "a better sight dead." She would drown hersolf that morning if she had the chance, Prisoner was remanded for a week RETURNED SOLDIERS AND THEIR MONEY.—.' A REGULAR
PREY FOR LOAFERS."

- Peter Scully. who is well known to the police. appeared at the Warrington Police Court on Friday on the charge of being drunk and disorderly in Dallam-lane at 7 40 the previ- ous night.— P S Evans said the prisoner was fighting another man,and both of them had received Injuries about the eyes. There were four men fighting altogether. In the presence of a large crowd and it was a most disgraceful affair.—The Chief Constable said prisoner was one of a number of young men who made that, end of the town hideous. A number of men came borne discharged from various "Tiny corps after taking part in the late war. They had a little money with them ' and the habitual loafers fairly devoured them while any of that lasted One of the men who went to the Pollee Station with the prisoner said he had returned after a long period of fighting for his country. He had several pounds upon him when be returned, and now be had only a few shillings left. Scully and a few others wanted to kill him for these few shillings, after he had spent the rest of the money on them. Prisoner was a regular Imfer and thief and a dangerous man in the town. Men coming home from the front caused no little trouble in the town owing to their foolish generosity. They were looked upon as legitimate ant regular nrev by loafers.—Prisoner waslsent to gaol for a month with hard labour. THE REORNT CYCLE PARAGE kT WARRINGTON.—A PROGRAMME SELLER'S DISHONESTY. Alfred Beckett, a youth familiarly known as " Lawyer" Beckett. appeared at the Warrington Police Court on Tues- day on tbe charge of stealing 105 94, the money of Charles Leigh, treasurer of the Cycle Parade and Carnival bed on August 23rd in aid of the Infirmary and Fltstriet Nursing Association.—Superintendent Monaghan said that on the day in question prisoner was instructed byladr John Blythe,local representative of the .• Liverpool Echo" to sell programmes i of the parade. He was provided with fourteen dozen and four programmes and his duty was to hand over the money realized by the sale of the programmes to Mr Blythe. He failed to do this and luring the evening Mr Blythe found him in a drunken condition. Prisoner made use of disgust- ing language when spoken to about ths money. He ab- sconded from the town and a warrant was issued. He was traced to Liverpool but the pollee then lost sight of him. At 10 15 on Monday evening, however, he (Superintendent Monaghan) saw the prisoner, who was drunk, riding about in a hansom smoking cigarettes. Prisoner was taken into custody and I made use of horrible language on the way to the Police Station. That morning he was charged with the offence and stated that he spent eight or nine shillings of the money and then left the town. A bad feature of the case was that the money had been obtained for a chiritable purpose. If prisoner had been honest be would hays received 44 93 for his day's work. It appeared that he subsequently joined the North Lancashire Militia at Preston —Prisoner now stated that he trusted other lads with the programmes and they never paid him —Superintendent Monaghan said that was Beckett's seventh appearance. He was incorrigible and worthless,and a wotle chatacter he (the Superintendent) did not know.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month with hard labour.

div.head: MINOR OASES.
div.p: MINOR OASES.
Warrington Borough Court.

FRlDLV—Before the deputy-mayor (In the chair). Councillor Smethinst and John RoJens, Messrs Young. Hepherd, and Thornton. A RETURNED SOLDIER AND HIS WIFE —Joseph Sherwood, tC Baxter.stre.t, was summoned for deserting his wife, Mary Ann Sherwood, 19, Gas-street —Mr Browne appeared for the complainant and Mr Jenkins represented tics defend- ant —Mr Browne said the defendant went out to South Africa as a reservist on October 10th. 1899. He returned three weeks ago and instead of going to his wife's apartments went to his brother's house. He was taken 11l and she nursed him for a fortnight, but he would not pay any money to her and she was perfectly helpless.—fie (Mr Browne) was instructed that the reserve pay which defendant received on his return amounted to over £lOO but he would not make an effort to maintain his wif..--Oomplainant,in her evidence, said the only reason defendant gave for his conduct was that she put a Volunteer's tunic on at a party last Christmas.—ln cross-examination she denied that she paraded the streets in a state of drunkenness whilst wearing the • tunic. She ad- mitted that defendant told her he would get a house, but he was taken ill. Fie then asked her to go and live with him at his brother's, but she refused.—The Bench considered that the desertion was not proved, and dismissed the case. WIFE Assarivr.--John Pownall, 39, Lord Nelson-street, was summoned for assaulting his wife, Catherine Pownall on September 9th —Defendant pleaded "guilty to assaulting complainant but not to striking her."—The magistrates clerk explained that defendant probably meant that he-' insulted" her.—Complainant stated that de'endant struck her in the face twice with his fist. —Defendant, who had previously been convicted for similar offences, was committed to prison for 14 days with hard labour.
