div.head: Runcorn Petty Sessions.
div.p: Runcorn Petty Sessions.
NoNDLY.—Before Mews _NV:rimming (In the chair), and J
Pritchard.

A HELSBY COMPANY'S APPLICA.TION.—Mr W Grunt, on behalf of the Red Sandstone Company lielsby applied for a license empowering them to keep mixed explosives.—As the anplieent had previously had a Unease but had allowed it to lapse inadvertently. The license was granted. Tag ATTEMPTED SUlClDE•—Hattnah Grubb, 18 White-it', was °barged on remand with attempting to commit suicide on the 23rd August. —The evidence which has already been reported was supplemented by the evidence of Sergeant Bottom who stated that the prisoner had had a spell of drinking prior to the attempt, and that when he got to the house the woman was in convulsions and was black in the facie. If he had not administered an emetic witness believed she would have died —The husband of the prisoner said he coul4 assign no reason why she attempted to take her life. He thought she was all right at the present time and was quite willing to take charge of her.—The magistrates deo;ded that the woman cad her husband Walter Grubb, should be bound over in the sum of £5 to be of good behaviour for six months. A QUARREL BETWEEN FATHERa.—Joseph Jolley. Peningron'a Row, was summened by James Gayter, of Norton-street, for an alleged assault committed on the 7th September.—The evidence showed that on the date in ques- tion the defendant's aoy ill used one of complainant's hens. Complainant struck the boy for his action and thenwent toltell the father.who assaulted complainant by striking him on the face and on the Abs.—Conflicting evidence was given, the defendant denying the eharge,—Jolley was fined 20a includ- ing costs or In default 14 days. A BELLIGERENT SEAMAN.—Thomas Cummings, able sea- man, was summoned for assaulting John William Harrison. second mate on the 13elphor, on the 13th inst. He plesdeci not guilty.—Complainant, whose bead was bandaged, said that the defendant joined the vessel about five months ago. On Saturday morning there was some trouble about the disgraceful state in which the men had left the foreoastle when they quitted the ship, which was in the lay-by. The chief officer told him to report the matter to the captain. He did so. and the captain spots to the men about it. Defendant accosted him (complainant) and said he had no right to send ordinary seamen to clean the forecastle. He told the man that he should use his discretion about the matter. Defen- dant then used obscene language and struck him in the neck. He lifted his stick to guard himself .and the boatswain took it from him. Defehdant then hit him an unexpected blow on the lett eye. The blow, wkiah he thought Was t o bard to have been struck with the fist, caused an open wound which bled considerably. A police constable took him to a doctor. Defendant swore that the complainant first struck him with a stick, Frederick Cooke, boatswain, corroborating the point.—The Captain of the vessel bore out the complain. ant's statement the Bench deciding that as the case was a very serious one the defendant must pay a flee of £3 and costs. The fine was paid. MINOR IDABEL—At these sessions Sarah Lewis (77), of 20a Regent-street, was summoaed for keeping a disorderly house from May let to September 10th. She was bound over in the stun of £5 to be of good behaviour for Six months. The Chairman said that it had not been for her age she would have been sent to prison.—William Morris, a tramp, was sent to gest for 14 days for begging in Bridge-street on Sunday. P 0 Wilding proved the case.—John Ward, Fryer-street, was fined 5s for using obscene language on September Bth. P 0 att proved the Case.

div.head: PROMISE v. PERFORMANCE.
div.p: PROMISE v. PERFORMANCE.

Of every thousand promises tr ade, how many are followed by the faithful performance of the thing pro- mised ? We are quite unable te lay, but take comfort , from the belief that nobody else is any better informed 'on the matter. Certainly there can be no doubt at all that broken promises are as plentiful as grains of sand by the seashore. That, unfortunately, is within the range of everybody's experience. We have all beard of the student who was exceedingly backward in paying his debts, and who, being in need of a reference to enable him to gain credit from a taller, applied to the rector of big college, wise wrote of him thug :—" Mr. -- is a very promising young man." When Mrs. M. A. Self. of Da, Pretoria-avenue, Wal- thamstowe, was suffering from acute indigestion, with all its attendant horrors, she was premieed, by medical authority, relief by using mustard poultices and sipping soda water and brandy. That prowl% has taken its proper place alongside some millions of its broken fellows. Mrs. Self's sufferings have at last tarminated ; but that happy result was achieved by aid of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and in no other way. Says, Mre. Self : " For months at a time I never knew what it was to properly digest my food Whatever I ate produced great pain it the chest, which ocoasionally was so acute that to draw a long breath was agony. Flatulence was a constant trouble to me. Often of a night it has caused me to it up in bed, and I was always badly punished whea I bad been foolish enough to eat a meat supper. On snob occasions I got no sleep at all, and was fit for nothing the next day. Constipation,too, of an obstinate nature added to my distremand was responsible,l believe.fer the languor and fits of drowsiness which constantly afflicted nae,pa r- ticularly after eating. When I yielded to the feeling,and slept during the, day, I awake dazsd and unrefreshed. It was while in this condition that an old man advised me to take Mother Seigel'a Curative Syrutt. He had hintself used it for yeare, and spoke very highly of it. Accept- ing his advice. I found to my delight th• relief which I had so long soucht. A few bottles quickly restored me ts health, and from that day to this it has been our family medicine. It is true that from time to time I I have had a slight return of my old malady, but on suck oceasinas one bottle has never failed to set me right again."

div.head: HOME FROM THE CAPE.
div.p: HOME FROM THE CAPE.
Liverpool Militia Arrive at Warrington.

On Monday morning the 3rd and 4th Battalions ef the King's Liverpool Regiment (Militia) arrived at Warring- an from South Africa where they have been serving,the 3rd battalion since December 1901 and the 4th Mace the early nart of this year. Thc battalions,which numbered over 1,000 officers and men, were under the command of Camel Batten and Lieutenant Colonel Hand respec- tively. They arrived at Bank Quay Station in two sections between six and eight o'cleck and were accorded a hearty reception. They matched to Orford Barracks headed by the band of the Depot, and were drawn up on the square. The colours of the regiment were then broug'ht from the officers' quarters and presented to the battalions, after which Colonel Batten briefly addressed the men. He con- grata' ated them on their safe return home, their excel- lent conduct in the fiat and their exemplary character whilst coming home. He trusted the regiment would al ways maintain the high standard it had attained in South Africa. _ _ _

At noon the Lord Mayor of Liverpool (Alderman Petrie) visited the barracks for the purpose of distribut- ing the South African medals to the returned soldiers. The two battalions assembled in the square, and the Lord Mayor, accompanied by Colonel Fitzberbert,Colonel Mount Batten. Captain Jacob, and other officers, pro- ceeded En a position midway between the battalions.

Colonel nizherbert said the Lord Mayor of Liverpool had kindly came down there to Rive a welcome to the men of the Liverpool Regiment on their return from South Africa. They all felt very glad indeed that he had come and shown by his presence the hearty recogaition of the city of Liverpool of the services of the 3rd and 4th Ballaliana in South Africa. The LORD MAYOR said he was very pleased to welcerne "che men home after the arduous" duties they had per- formed for their country: They were all highly pleased at the result of the war in South Africa. Although that result was anticipated years ago,they had ne idea what- ever that the war would have lasted as long as it had done. He was sure that for the;grand result of the war they were highly indebted te the men who had gone to the front and fought the battles of their country, and to nose More, he thoueht. than to the men whit had been attached to The Kine'd (r.iverpool Regiment). They had done their duty nobly, and on all hands he had been told that their duties had been well performed. He was sure the people of Liverpool and the people of Lanca- shire, in fact all the people of this country were greatly indebted to these MAR for the way they had performed that duty. As chief magistrate of the city of Liverpool, he welcomed them home that day, and he hoped they would find that those who were near and dear to them whom they had left 133 hind, had been well looked after while they had been away. Fle was sore that the public had dose all they possibly could to look after those they had left behind. He hoped the man would all be able to find employment, and settle down to their work as they had done in the past. Colonel MOUNT BATTEN, who addreseed the company as the " Liverpool Linnet t," said be called them by that old title because he wished to :show to his lordship how much they appreciated their connection with that mag- nificent city of which he was chief magistrate. They had unfortunately been more or less divided from it for seme time, but he was happy to say that they were now drawing together again, a proof ef which was that his lordship had taken the trouble to travel there, and wel- come them on their return from foreign service. It was an act of grace on his part which they thoroughly appr,_ dated, and which would draw them nearer to the grand city of which he was chief megietrate. On behalf of the two battalions. he thanked his lordship for his kind- WWI in being there that day. The Smth Afrinan medals were then distributed, after which' the Lord Mayor was entertained at luncheon by the officers of Orford Barracks:

ARRIVAL IN LIVERPOOL. The Liverpool men iPft Warrington during the after- noon and on arrival at the City were eordially welcomed home by their relatives and friends Outside the station several thousand people wer3 congregated, and there was a very enthusiastic scene when the men Came into Ranelagh-street and were recognised. In anticipation of the arrival of the battalions, a crowd of people were gathered in Ranelazh-street as early as ten o'clock, and shortly before four many thousands of people were pre- sent. A number of police were on duty to regulate the traffic. About thirty of the men reside in Warrington and were cordially welcomed by their relatives and friends.

div.head: WARRINGTON v BRIGHOUGR RANGRRS.
div.p: WARRINGTON v BRIGHOUGR RANGRRS.

The spectators who gathered round the Wilderspool enolosure on Aaturday &item° m experienced lon ir sad weary wait of threequarters of an hour, ere the Bangers put in an appearance. The visitorsf were timed to reach the Central Station at ten minutes to three.but they had the misfortune to miss the connection at Manchester and did not arrive in Warrington until ten minutes to four. The fingers of the clock pointed to quarler past that hour before operations were commenoed. The teams turned out as selected and were ts follows :

Warrington. Knight, back; Fish, Hookenhall, Dickenson, and Harris, three-quarter backs ; Burgess and B 'mends, half-backs ; Morrison, Boardman, Roberts, W Swift, J Swift, Forster. Edmondson and Taylor. forwards. Brighouse Rangers : Hartley. back; Chappell, Bevan. Sutcliffe and Walker, three-quarter backs • Rose and Crowther, half-backs ; Miller, Woffanden, KR- burn. Whitelaw, Hodgson, Walton, and Banket,forwards. Referee : Mr W Robinson. danninghana. Touch judges : Messrs T H Houghton (St Heiens). and W zones (Runcorn). Fish lost the spin of the cola, an 4 the Rangers' captain eTected to play with the strong breeze behind his men in the first half. Taylor kicksd off. After the preliminary exchanges, Harris was called upon to check an attempt by Walker to break through. The home forwards dribbled away to centre, where a number of scrimmages took place. Edmonds got away cles,riv, but n' passing movement was clumsily taken up by Dickenson and Harris. and the effort was easily frustrated. Crowther kicked to Knight and that player replied by finding touch in mid-field. Burgess led another passing movement, and Fish tried to break through but failed. By making good use of the wind and taking advantage of the punt into touch rule, Brighouse got down to the Warrington end. Ross secured from the pack, but stepped into touch when near the line Knight c'eared his lines effectively and further ground was gained when Fish got possession and by a run and kick removed play to midfield. A miss- pass by Burgess gave Mallinson a clear field. Be dribbled over the lle. out Dickenson out-paced him, and robbed him of what seemed a certain try by kicking dead. The drop out gave no relief to the Warrington man, for scrimmage followed scrimmage with such painful monotony near the home line that the spectators gave any attempt to open out the game ironical cheers. Warringtoa defended well and the visitors were forced beyond half way. first Knight find- ing touch at half way, and subsequently Fish with a couple of judicious punts forcing scrimmages near the quarter flag. Exchanges between Crowther and Knight saw the Warrington custodian badly fouled, and a free kick to the home men saw Boardman, Morrison, B.imarm awl Fish all experience the hardest of luck in not effecting a score after a dashing passing movement. The visitors got oat of the difficulty by finding touch. A round of passing by the Warrington backs again platted Warrington on the aggres- sive and Fish was palpably obstructed by Chappell ere he could get the ball from Hock:sal/all. At half time there was a clean score sheet.

Warrington pressed severely in the second half, and Fish almost plaeed a goal from a penalty, the ball striking the upright. A round of passing was upset by Sutcliffe who intercepted a pass to Fish. when the way to the line seemed clear. On several occasions Fish over ran Hockenhall, and even tually Fish decided to operate behind the scrimmage Bdminds going centre three-quarter and gochenhall Hartley and Orowther took full advantage ef the punt-out rule, and scrimmage followed scrimmage with such regular- ity as to rob the play of any interest. The Manger 3 seemed well content to make a draw, and It looked as though there would be no scaring. In the last few minutes of the match the unexpected happened. The home forwards dribbled down the field. and T Swift picking up the ball threw it across to Marris, who receded Hartley, and scored a try near the corner flag. Fish failed at the place kick. Score ,—Warriug- ton. cue try (3 Points) ; Brighouse, nil.

ARADFORD V. RUNCORN This match at Park Avenue on Saturday was attended by about B,COO spectators. Bradford were short of Marsden at half, and gave S N Poster. their Bristol recruit, a trial. Carrell, formerly of Batley, also came into the team in place of Grayson. Runcorn were as advertised. Broadley lost the toss, and had to kick off against a strong wind towards the Park. Runcorn at the outset had the best of matters, and used touch with better judgment and effect than the Bradford men. There was some good forward work shown on both sides, but tke visiting backs (notably Ploughton) were the better. The latter, from a mark by Butterworth, landed a goal with a long kick—the only score up to the interval On the change of ends Bradford had the wind. but Old not make much use of it, being out-manceevred by Runaorn. The only feature of interest in this half was a grand penalty goal. kicked by Mosby from a difficult angle near the centre. Result :—Bradford, 1 goal (2 points) ; Runcorn, 1 goal (2 points). Teams. Runcorn—Houghton. back; Jones, Butterworth, Warder, and Ylanlgan. three-quarter beaks; Jolley and Richardson, half backs; Walker, Farmer. Woods, Reece, Lightfoot, Moulton. Higgins, and Williams. forwards.

Bradford—Ward: back; Pollard. Mosby, Dunbavln, and Rinton, three-qoarter backs • Heseltine and Foster, half backs ; Smedley (capt ), Laidiaw, F Smales, 13 Smales• Carroll, Turner, Sharratt. and Robertson, forwards. WIDNRB v. HaTLIIY.T2 This match was played at Widnes. before 2,500 people. After some pretty passing by the Widnes threequarters Taylor hesitated when he had a clear field, and lost a grand chance, the ball going dead. lihortly afterwards Taylor failed at a place. Wilson picked up grandly from a Widnes dribble, but lost the chance by a bad punt. From a sorummage near the uprights Taylor landed a splendid goal. Wilson let Widnes through, but Fitzgerald. who was repeatedly notice- able for good play, saved the situation. Widnes now pressed, but did not make the most of their calmness. Taylor was just etoppe i close to the One. Batley were new making titre 'EMUS efforts, and Aspey kicked a second goal. Half-time—Widnes 2 goals (4 polnts). Batley nothing. Aspey re-started, arid progress was at once made, Widnes were penalissd for faulty scrummage work. and Fitzgerald got Die leather well down the field, Wilson making more progress with a mark. The venue was then changed, but Wilson neatly frustrated a daring dribble by the Widnes forwards. Douglas spoiled by ten much kicking, and the visitors were let Into the Widnes line. Taylor relieved the pressure. but Oakland and Fitzgerald passed prettily. and Kershaw received, being held up on the line. Davies attempted to place from a mark. Batley were new holding their ground well, and Davies whipped acroes the field, recovering a pass from Midgl.y intended for Fitzgerald, and beat the Widnes backs, scoring in the corner. The same player failed at the kick. Davits scored another try under the posts a few minutes later, and landed a goal. Result : —Batley 1 gal, 2 tries (2 points), Widnes 2 goals (4 points). Teams:—
_ Batley—Wilsort. balk:Davies. Goodall. Lillny,and Kershaw, three-quarters ; Oakland and Mldgley, half backs; Wolsten- bohne, Mossiev, Dews, Spurr, Phillips, Judge, Hough, and Thomas. forwards.

Widnes—Kinsella. bank: 'Julien, Rown. Whelan, and Tilley, three touters ; A. Taylor and Douglas, halt backs ; Aspev, Moss, Webster, Riley, Rigby, Leystioa, Power, and Curtis, forwards. HUDDERSFIIILD y ST IMAMS. --- • - -

, Huddersfield played their first match of the season at Far- town. before 4,000 spectators Prescott was absent from the St Helens pack, and his place was taken by McGuire, and Moseley took the place of Larard at centre 112 the Huddersfield team. The visitors won the toss. and played with the wind at their backs. Sutcliffe kicked off. and no return was made. St Helens were soon attacking. the Brothers Dewhirst and Moseley relieving the pressure. Foulkes got held near the line. and passed to Mooney, who traryggerred to Green, and he scrambled ever the line and scoraff. Lee made a poer attempt at goal. Half-time score :—St Helens 1 try (3 points), Huddersfield nil

Lee restarted,but a scrummage was formed at the half-way for off-side. A good kick by Moseiey gave Huddersfield an opportunity. Kitchen got hold.andlfter a strong run scored for the home team, Sutcliffe falling to add the extra points. Huddersfield were now making good use of the wind. Barnes got away, but could not get past the half-way line, being tackled by Kitchen. Readyhough had his kick charged, and Lee getting held ran, but stuck to the ball too lone, throwing away an easy chance of scoring. A lot of long kicking took place. Foalkes giving his side the advantages From a scrum- mage Kitchen got away, but was tackled by Barnes. Beady- hough put in a long kick, and following up well prevented any return. F Dewhirst got hold, and after passing by Kitchen. Moseley, W Dewhirst, and Deere. the latter scored a try near the posts, and Sutollffe converted. Hunter made a good run, but we, brought don by Readyhough in the home half. Result : —Huddersfield 1 goal and 2 tries (8 points), St Helens 1 try (3 points). Muddersfield —Readyhough, back ; Deere. W Dewhirst, Moseley, and Kitchen, three-quarter backs ; F Dewhirst and A Marsden ; half backs; Barrowclough, Chambers, Dawson: Driver, Knight, Littlewbod, Naylor, and Sutcliffe (captain). forwards.

Helens—Porter, back ; Liyersedne. Barnes, Doherty, Mid Ranter, three-quarter backs ; Foulkes and fienneday, half backs; Briers, Lee, Mooney, Carney, Whiteley, Thomp- son. McGuire, and Green, forwards.

div.head: HULL RrNGSTON ROVERS V. LEIGH.
div.p: HULL RrNGSTON ROVERS V. LEIGH.

The appearance at the first match on the Rovers' ground of the team which lowered the colours of the champions was a great attraction, consequently the Craven-street enclosure contained a crowd of fully 8,090 people. Leigh played the touch-line game to seine purpose, and Ganley was the first to score. Towers failing at goal. The game was equalised by Cole with a try for the Rovers, which Smith failed to convert Before half-time Johnson scored, and Towers ki .tked a goal. so that Leigh led by 1 goal. 2 tries (8 points) to 1 try (3 points.) After the interval j Riley 'distinguished himself by placing two tries to the credit of Leigh, while Dunbavin took the bell from ascrumnage and dropped it neatly between the ports. The Rovers, save for a spurt or two, gave an indifferent display. They were absolutely outplayed by a superior team, and Leigh won by 2 goals and 4 tries (1.8 paints) to Mall Kingston Hovers, 1 try (3 points).

div.head: WIGAIf V SALFORD.
div.p: WIGAIf V SALFORD.

Salford representatives; visited Wigan. where in pre- vious years they have invariably met with reverses. Fortu- nately for them, they found the Central Park organisation with a weakened contingent, due to the absence of Barr and Deicersley. who are on the injures' list. The vacancies were filled by Downs and Brooks. In the first half of the hostilities. which were of an even description, the home club had the misfortune to hate Rouse damaged, and after his retirement Salford, as the outcome of a scrambling forward movement, =weeded in scoring Riley crossing the line and Griffiths landing a goal. Result —Salford, 1 goal, 1 try (5 points) ; Wigan, nil.

div.p: SWINTOX • OLDHAM

The meeting of these teams at Swinton was looked forward to with Intense interest by the sopporters of each club, and fully 12,000 spectators were present when the match was started. Swinton gradually assumed the upper hand, and Cooper gaining possession ran half the length of the field and scored a grand try for Preston to convert. Shortly after- wards A Lees made his mark close in. and Nerguson placed a goal. Swinton, however, played better still afterwards, and Morgan gathering from the pack dropped a goal. At half- time Swinton led by 2 goals and 1 try (7 points) to Oldham 1 goal (2 points).—Resuming, the game was not more than three minutes old when Preston picked up smartly and kicked up the field, and Wallwork following up passed to Barnett, who scored, Preston from a difficult position landing a goal, Cooper moored after splendid combination by the home backs. but Preston failed at goal, and the result was— Swinton 3 goals and 3 tries (15 points), to Oldham 1 goal (2 points.)

div.p: BROUGHTON RANGERS V HULL.

This match took place'at %Theater's Field,Broughton,before 10,000 spectators. The home side were without W James, and Barnett took his place at half-back, whilst in the Hall team, JacquJa had to play at full back owing to Taylor being on the injured list. Broughton Rangers 1 goal and 6 tries (17 points), Hull 1 try (3 points.) HUNSLET T HALIFAX: THE PARKSIDERS' THIRD DEFEAT. About 7,000 spectators witnessed the opening game of the season at Parkside, Hunslet. The contest was exciting and hard fought, and favoured with capital weather conditions, it proved disappointingly poor in the quality of the football. The house forwards played a good hard game, but the best features of the struggle were contributed by the Halifax back division. The first half ran somewhat against the yid- tors,for whom. however. This match wee played on the ground of the first named, Sankey kicked off against a strong wind and immediately the visitors became aggressive, F. Hare scoring two goals in quick succession. Half-time, Arpley Juniors two goals, Sankey Green, nil. Playing with the wind behind them the homesters soon made matters warm for the visitors who rarely crossed the half-way line. H Burns with a good shot opened the scoring for Sankey. Soon afterwards a rush by the Sankey forwards forced Hudson to kick through his own coal making the scores equal. Nelson started play for St Peter's against a slight breeze but failed to get through. The home team got possession and from a bit of goad play scored. Half-time. Newchurch Villa 1, St Peter's nil. WARRINGTON SANKEY ALBION 9 V HIGHFIELD TANNERY.

This match was played at Runcorn on Saturday, and after a rough and exciting game, the Athlone cams out on top by two goale to nil. Pugh scoring both goals. LANCASHIRE CUP. EARLESTOWN V WHITE STAR WANDERERS.

In the first match at home this season Earlostown met the White Star Wanderers, the competition being that of the first round of the Lancashire Cup. There was a good crowd of spectators, numbering close on 1,500. many of whom were attracted to witnass the performance of the new " talent " recently acquired by the local club. The visitors were quite outclassed and Harlestown won by twelve goals to one.
TMB COMBINATION. MIMIC V NEWTON.

This match was .ledde-a--Or; the irt;;;rid of the Welsh club on Saturday. A Most amusing scene was witnessed just before the kick-off, as a hare ran across the ground and both players and spectators ran after it but they found It too smart for them. James put the ball in motion for Mirk against a rather powerful wind. The home forwards at once made tracks for their opponents' goal, but they were cleverly pulled up. The opening exchanges were of a very even character, and twice the visitors were very dangerous but they failed to get through. Harris got well away on the Ohirk left wing but a splendid centre was not taken advant- age of. Notwithstanding considerable interference by the wind, the game was very keenly contested- The Lancashire team playing with goal combination twice penetrated the Ohirk goal the Welshmen only being able to register one point. In tte second halt the home team secured the advantage, scoring three times and winning the game by tour goals to two.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

Benefit Concert in the Co-operative Hall. The Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, was almost filled on Monday evening when a concert, promoted by Mr Tich Thomas, humorist, for the bentit of the widow and children of the late Joan Fairhurst, Latchford, was held. An interesting and varied programme was submitted, and the efforts of the artistes, who gave their services were highly ap- preciated. The opening iteln was a pianoforte solo which was efficiently rendered by Mr Bert Smith. Miss Emily F flitebin, of Liverpool, very sweetly sang "The Star of Bethlehem" and was cordially applauded. Later in the evening she gave a feeling interpretation of "Aileen Animals." Master Tom Barton contributed two violin solos in a manner highly creditable for so young a per- former. Mr 11 0 Hughes delighted the audience with his effective rendition of "The Holy City" and in response to an encore sang "Gwiti 1 y Delyn ;the land of the harp.)" Mr P Smith sang" I never can forget " and " Though fortune darkly o'er me frowns " which were well received. Mr J F Bur- rows proved himself an adept at sleight-of-baud, and his entertainment was elle of tho most popular items. The humorous element was well sustained by Mr Tich Thomas, Mr J Williams Mr W J Jones, and Mr P Burke, whose efforts to amuse were completely successful. In addition to several humorous selections, Mr Williams provided one of the most acceptable features ot the concert in his song "The blind collier " wnich was excep- tionally well rendered. Mr Burke was heartily recalled for the song " How to love, by One who knows " which created considerable mirth. Mr Thomas gave "D, you kao* any more funny stories ?" in capital style, and Mr Jones's "on parade " was warmly received, Master Lang con- tributed " The honeysuckle and the ,Bee." The accompaniments were ably supplied by Mr Bert Smith and Mr W Looker

div.head: LATE MR. E. W. T. RICHMOND.
div.p: THE LATE MR. E. W. T. RICHMOND.
Memorial Service at St. Paul's Church.

A large congregation assembled in St Paul's Church on Sunday morning when a memorial tter- vies was held to the late Mr E W T Richmond, managing director of the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Company, and also to the late Mr Thomas Beckett, a passenger porter who was knecked down by a light engine at the Central Station and killed. A large number of the late Mr Richmond's employes attended as a mark of respect to their late chief, and there were alge present a number of railway servants from the Coati-al Statiom. The service commenced with the singing of "Lead, kindly Light," and at the close Mr Wilkes, the orgaitist. played the Dead March in " Saul," the congregation standing meanwhile. The service was conducted by the Rev W Brace- camp (vicar), who preached from the words" flow wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan ?" Joremih 112 c., 5v.) They had met that morning, he said, under very sad circumstances, ?tamely, to mourn the loss of two friends. It might be that outsiders were asking why such a service should be held in St. Paul's Church. and why these immediately associated with the deceased had been invited to be present that morning. He would tell them. The officers of that church and many others in Warring- ton felt that Mr. Richmond's loss was a terrible one, and that it was their duty to meet together to sympathize with his widow as well as with the family of tke unfortunate men who was killed at the station. By the death of Mr. Richmond the town had lost a wonderful business man ; it would in fact be difficult to find his equal, and Warring- tea was the pcterer for his loss. The double memorial servire that morning was held to enable them to sympathize with one another in the Reuse of God, where they could offer their united prayers, and also derive useful and important lessons from the mad fatalities which had so recently occurred. It was a strange coincidence that both departed friends were killed by accident. They had one man killed while riding a bicycle end another man killed while carrying on his work ea the railway. The preacher proceeded to show in an interesting way that the swelling of Jordae was typical of death. However much they might engege themselves in business, they must realise that death like Jordan was constantly flawing. Just as the late Mr Richmond seemed at the height of his prosperity, just as everything, so far as his business was- concerned, was flourishing and the harvest time had arrived, then the river of death overflowed. We wanted more men like Mr Richmond at the present time. He (the preacher) would ask them to make un for this terrible loss and to more fully realise their respon- sibility. bet them also remember that they were in the bands of God, a God who overruled every- thing. 7he preacher proceeded to refer to the im- portance of sanctifying and preparing themselves for heaven. They must not leave the eoul's salva- tion until the end. They must make up their minds that if they wanted to enjoy the advantages and privileges of heaven they must begin it here down below. If the removal of their two friends led those present to lead better and nobler lives then their death, though so sad and sudden, would have been of the utmost importance and weuld be a source of great blessing to them as individuals.

The great vine at Hampton Court Palace, now 134 years old, is looking at its best with its crop of Hambro' grapes, destined for use at the King's table. This veer, in order to give the vine a rest, some 2.000 or 3,000 bunches were thinned out, leaving only 700 bunches to mature, instead of the usual crop of 1,200.

div.head: IMPRESSIONS OF WARRINGTON AND SANKEY BRIDGES.
div.p: IMPRESSIONS OF WARRINGTON AND SANKEY BRIDGES.
A Manchester Cyclist's Visit to Hale.

On one of the fine days of last week, says the writer of " Cycling Notes " in the "Manchester Guardian ", I went on a good long ride into Lancashire, to a plane that is, Rfancy, seldom visited by Manchester riders, though it is no doubt well known to those of West 'Lancashire. Some of the country that I traversed is ' very dull ; but Hale, the objective of my journey, is such • delectable place that I have no hesitation in recommending my readers to follow in my wheelmarks. It is • village on the Lancashire bank of the Mersey. chiefly composed of whites,' %shed cottages with green lattice porches. Some of the cottages are thatched, many are fronted by bright gardens, and one, half-timb9rld, is inscribed "R. 1665 E." At the east end of the village there is a p'cturesque old house of red brick with red stone facings. smothered in ivy and flanked by a deep orchard. Now it serves as a farmhouse, bat one would judge by the armorial :bearings ab3ve its tall, narrow doorway that it was. once a manor-house. In front of it the read bends between Lombardy poplars to the church—a plain red sandstone building with a tewer—and then, developing into a gated lane, runs down between cornfields to a lighthouse above the fore- shore. On the south side of the churchyard a large flat stone, marking the grave of the " Chltde of Hale," is inscribed in this wise Here Lyeth the Body of John Middleton'the Child° : Nine Peet Three : Born d 1578 : Dvede 163."

There is a pleaeing view of the Frodsham hills and the edge of He!shy between the limes that border this sunny side of the churchyard, and from the lane that goes down to the water one sees something of Hale Hall, a charming red sandstone manaion with bays and wings relieved in parts with ivy. From the lighthouse the prospect is wider still, though how wide on a clear dav I cannot say. For last Tuesday the Cheshire shore was veiled in a midsummer-like haze, and my memory of a former visit is not sufficiently vivid to enable me to speak with exactness. Bet whereas I seem to remember having seen Moel Famtnau then. en Tuesday even the high lands of Frodsham acid Efelsby, togetlaer with Mount Manisty, loomed more like cloud 1 than land. and Stanlow Point and Pool Rocks were unrecognisable. Up- stream even Runcorn Bridge was blurred, while down- stream one could see no further than Oglet Point and a black mass which I took to be the woods about Soeke. 1 There is another and smaller wood nearer the lighthouse r and in it a duck decoy.

But I must turn bacik for a space in order to tell how reached Hale. On the far side of New Bridge Hollow highway, and afterwards lead a I forsook the Chester capital run through Bellington and Lymm and Thelwall. The morning was glorious, and a following wind he'ped me up Agden Brow. At Lvmm I felt tempted to put up my bicycle and traverse the pleasant footpath along the far side of the dam, for the waters, slightly ruffled by the breeze, and the church overlooking them made a brave show in the sunlight. But.reeisting. I halted not, nor yet at the next village, where an inseription on the inn tells the wayfarer that"ln the year 920 King Edward the Elder ferinded a city here and called it Thelwall." Beyond Thelwall the road runs alongside the Man- cheater Ship Canal for a space, and then, at Latchford. crosses it by a swing bridge. Up to this point the road is good, but beyond the bridge macadam is exchanged for eetts. They also are of decent quality, bat the tram- lines, continuous all the way from Latehford to Sank,V Bridges—el ase on three miles,—are in places set so near to the kerb as to be awkward, while in wet weather the " going " must be decidedly tricky. In one place the street runs alongekle the inky Mersey, and further on a bridge, dangerously narrow for the considerable traffic that it has to bear, carries one across the river. Looking at the turbid Mersey from this the only bridge between Warburton and Runcorn it is hard to believe that a century ago there was good salmon fishing at Warrington. The traveller. who is intent en the Liverpool road, as I was, may avoid the narrew streets in the heart of the town by turning sharply to the left on the far side of the bridge. The road, macadamised, passes through a square in which there are some Ruesian guns, captured in the Crimea, and then bends to the right over a level crossing. Im- mediately beyond the eressinee one should again turn to the left, along Wilion-Patten-atreet. Further on the way bee& to the right between a hotel and another railway station, and then vises easily to Sankey-street, the local name for a part of the Manchester-en-Liverpool " turnpike.' Turning to the left at the junction, one crosses the London and North-Western main line by a bridge, and presently, a hundred yards or see beyond the bridge, reaches a fork. The right-hand way looks the likelier, for whereas it is broad and maeadamised, the left-hand one is narrow and paved. The latter is our way, how- ever. and a very ugly one it is as far as Sankey Bridges, a mile or so away. Fcr some distance it is bordered on one side by works and forges that remind one of the Black Country, and most of the houses on the rest of the way are mean and grimy. Beyond Sankey Bridges —a place of foul smells—WV:l gains the open road, with lig great stacks of te'egraph wires. Away on the left , Haltonillill,created by theblack ruins of its osstle,breaks the skyline, and s glance over one's left shoulder reveals the green slopes of Walton Hill. A short distance beyond Sankey Brideee I turned off the highway to the left, for the double purpose of re- newing an old acquaintance with the village of Penketh and gaining Farnworth by a slightly more direct way than that by Great Sankey and Bold. With the road itself I had no fault te find, but the country—chiefly corn land—ewes a little depressing. It is flat and shadowed by the vile smoke of Warrington or Widmer, according to the direction of the wind. The corn, mostly in stook, was more black than golden. I kept straight on through Penketh and then, near the Dern Inn, on the outskirts of Farnworth, crossed a railway bridge and at once here to the left. From s crossways on the edge of the village ef Farnwertb I kept a straight course along Derby-road, and on reaching a cemetery bore te the left. Later, phortly after I had crossed a paved bridge over Ftrnworth station and when I was within sight of Appleton Church, I turned to the right along a bread read, and at a fork 300 yards or so further on again went to the right. All this time I had the evil chimneys of Widnes in view, and pre- gently I rode through an extremely ill-favoured place— Ball Ditto's. At a crossways at the end sf it one arm of a fineerpoet—which, like others in the neighbourhood, would be better for repainting—vnarke the way to Hale. bank and Hale to the left. Thence the way was straight through Ditton—which rivals its neighbour Ball Ditton for squalor—and Halebank to the charming old village of my quest. Though the road itself was mostly good,exeept through Ball Ditton and onward to Halebank, there was little to Meese between the last-named place and Warrington. But the wiry to Hale is justified, as it were, by the end, and for this reason I have been at soma pains to make it clear. I had no sootier left Htlebank in the rear than I was gladdened by the familiar din of a mower,and in the field from which it came half a hundred pheasants were pecking among the golden stubble. Hares also abound, and partridges, too, in the fields right and left of this mile long road between Halebank and Hale. One enters the village, as one reaches the church, through poplars. From the church I rambled to the shore, arriving in time to see the last of a flotilla of barges on their way under canvas from Runcorn to Liverpool. Flecks of seagulls were scavenging the runnels and pools left by the out- going tide, which downstream was glorified by a broad wake of silver sunlight. I waited to see two tugs, each with five or six barges in tow, pass side by side close inshore. When presently they changed their course, heading for the Cheshire side, so that one saw them end on, they made a truly fine picture. They wore followed by a solitary smack under sail. The sun was redden- ing when I left the Lightheuse,and later, when I turned into ace of the thatched cottages to tea, the village fathers were meditating over theis evening pipes and the village lads were at cricket in the squire's park. A vermilion reaping-machine—mower and binder in one— drawn by two staunch chestnuts came rattling home from a field. The moon, well up in the sky, was light and a few wisps of clmd burned a dull red. It was lamp-time when I left Hale, and the moon was over- taken by a cloud. Now and again it made a pretence at struggling through, but it did not shine again that night. Inreerad of returning through Penketh I turned to the left when I had crossed the railway bridge near the Horn lon and ran on ts the Liverpool and Warring. ten highway, joining in at Bold. The forges on the way into Warrington were in full blast, lurid and steaming, clanging and smoking—an inferno in little. At the swing bridge at Latchford I had to wait with half-a dozen other cyclists for a ship to go by. By this time the wind had freshened, and although it was only a lean one, it made the uphill stretches hard. Later my back tyre gave out, luckily a short mile from home.

div.head: Feathers Hotel.
div.p: The Feathers Hotel.

At the County Borough Police Court on Monday, Mr Staiiley Wilson, applied for temporary authority for Richard Kendrick Williams to sell at the 1 Feathers Hotel, Bridge-street. He said Mr Williams was the manager appointed by the Liverpool 1 Public-house Trust Company. His character bad been furnished to the Chief Constable,who no doubt weuld have something to say about the matter. The:Chief Constable said Mr Williams wee a gentle- man eminently fitted for the licence. He recently completed a distinguished career in the army by a period of active service at the front. He attained almost the highest non-commissioned rank possible for a soldier te attain by good conduct. He left the army with a character marked as exemplary— the highest mark given. In physique he was also fitted to act the role of a " boniface." The scheme on which the house was to be conducted was a very good one, and he (Mr Talbot) would watch its developments with considerable interest.l--The Chairman (Ur F Monks) hoped the experiment woul Ibe a great euccess.—The application was I granted.

WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVE CLURS' MAINS.

The annual main in connection with the Warrington Conservative Club was commnoced on Saturday, but as there was so many cimnetitors it was found impossible te finish before dusk. The remainder of the games will therefore be played to-day Saturdiy. The consolation prizes will also b 3 competed for. The cliitribution will take place in the evening. A similar main in connection with the Junior Consirvative Club took place on the same day, and in this ease also the whole of the gaol" were not finished. Some gool play was witnessed on etch green by a large number of spectators. Fortunately the weather was favourable.

The Thelwall Nuisance.—Mr Naylor Still Persistent.

Sir.—l have just read the " Runcorn Notes" by your correspondent on the question of the tannery nuisance at Thelwall. The observations are just what any reasonable minded man would make from a superficial view of the present situation. The nuisance from Messrs f.ong's tannery which the Council's special expert, Dr Penny.tdescribed " as un- questionably dangerous and a fruitful source of much fatal cisease '' is still in evidence. Only yesterday the stench proceeding from the tannery was very vile in- deed.

Knowing the whole facts of the case, when the Coun- cil decided upon taking some action with respect to the drainage and water supply,' claimed the statutory notice co that I could he represented by an expert. This was not granted me but the work was hurried through in quite an expeditious manner which is quite out of keep- ing with Um usual snail-like act!oa of this unenviable authority. The report presented, is in such a form that any one, except those intimately acquainted with the precise condition of affairs would be drawn into the same error as your correspondent respecting Mr de Prez' report on the drainage question. The pulllic sewers have so frequently been coupled with my name that the general public confused our private drainage system with them. In this particular instance there is a want of distinctness and the two are muddled together in the ;usual fashion the general affairs of the Runcorn Rural District Council are Mr de Prez' report Is such a sweeping condemnation of the Council's 'own sewers that they are displaying the most extraordinary agility in putting matters right before they are called to task by their superiors. The water question is in a bigger meddle, for while the Council's analyst certifies the water is exceedingly good the bacteriological ex- amination which last year condemned one sample now states it is this year " one of remarkable purity." As regards the drainage on my property the Council's officials have had a free hand irom the first and I under- took to carry out any suggestion of improvment, if such could he made. _ . . .
You ccrrespondent has got :hcld of the real point at issue. _ _

=4" The Council have not discovered the origin of the ' horrible, acrid smell which prostrates r,those who inhale It?" I am afraid the Council do not wish this unpleasant truth to come out ; if they did I could give them the way, to find out the exact thing. If the Council will only engage a few more men like Dr Penny and Mr de PrEz,or say, substitute these two temporarily in place of Dr Adams and Mr Farrington they would soon succeed in" laying " the nuisance of which we have so long complained and which will continue to bring destruction on the neiglitourhood. Does any sane man suppose I would have left my house with all its interests and asscciations if a drain or a well was the cause of the nuisance, which a few pounds would have put right ? Let me quote from a letter in my possession from a gentleman whose wife was paralised by this stench and had to carried to a carriage. He has been chosen as one of three Sanitary Experts to give evidence before the Royal Commission on sewage now sitting :—" The smell referred to is not a sewage smell at all, but is entirely and absolutely due to the tannery operations carried on at Messrs Long's works." The residents of the district know this, including yours truly R. A. NAYLOR, St. Michael's House, Eoecton Gardens, London, S.W., September 18thZ1902t

div.head: AN OMNIBUS "TRUSTS"
div.p: AN OMNIBUS "TRUSTS"
(BY A CONDUCTOR.)

Mr. ALBEET NIIETON. formerly a London General Omnibus conductor, tel the "Weekly Dispatch "that the empios Si of the different companies and the officials of their union are keenly watching for the probable effect upon drivers and conductors of the inevitable "eombinewhich will sooner or later take place between the “London General" and the "Road Car" companies. Mr Nurton is a representativ.i man, and his reminisc- ences are of interest

"Few omnibus passengers," said he., "know the hours worked by drivers and conductors, and the terrible strain they have to bear. Exposure to all weathers needs a man as strong as a horse. I would not be equal to it myself if I were not fortified with what I recommend to All outdoor workers— Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people. London fogs and wet caught held of me, and I was laid up with pneu- monia. I was working fifteen hours a day, with an hour for meals. I suddenly felt a terrible pain in my side, and all night was in terrible agony. My cotton, who found I had pleurisy, wouldn't hear at my leaving bed. Atithe end of a month he let me get out of bed, but as I walked to the chair on the heartbrug I felt a pain, and before I could move a step I Mt something snap, as it were, inside me. When the doctor came he said I had inflammation of the bladder. I strgered agonies, day and night. I went to the Middlesex Hospital at the beginning of February, and afterwards to the University College Hospital, where after being examined under ether I was told my case was chronic, and I should be a confirmed invalid. I gradu- ally tent over until I looked like an old man. Besides the other pains I was never free from headache, and the very sight of food made me sick. I read in the newspapers of a lady who tad been cured in a very miraculous manner by Dr. Williams' pink pills. I tried them. ady four <lags after I commenced taking Dr. Williams' pink pills I got out of bed by myself, stood up, and put my clothes on. I felt so well that I went fore walk, and asked for breakfast. I am prepared to swear this before any judge in the world. Before I got to the end of the first box of Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people I was a different man. I persevered, and everybody Came in to see with their own eyes what a wonderful cure had been brought about." Mr Nurton and his wife now have a little laundry business at 198, Ksusingtan Park-road, London. This is one cf the instances in which cases incurable by ordin- ary medicine have been unquestionably cured by the remedy named, which can be obtained wherever medi-; cktlis a cld for two stillings and ninepence,

div.head: HARVEST FESTIVALS.
div.p: HARVEST FESTIVALS.
Ellesmere-street Wesleyan _ Chapel.

Harvest thanksgiving cervices were held In this place of worship on Sunday, and were exceptionally well at- tended. The preacher for the day was Mr W Light. At the afternoon service a children's choir rendered tha hymn "The spring-tide hour" in a very pleasing manner ; Miss. Annie Taylor presiding at the harmonium. In the evening Mr John Hulse was in charge of the in- erument. Miss Pattie Taylor accompanied the children on the pianoforte as they sang " Tell me the old, old story and " What shall the harvest be ?" As a dis- I missal hymn the choir sang "Count your blePsines." The collections for the day amounted to £2 63 10d. On Monday evening a successful fruit banquet and concert took place presided over by Mr John Barlow. The fol- lowing items were capitally gone through :—Pianoforte solos by Miss Pattie Taylor, recitations by Miss Gre7snn, songs by Mr,Norton, song by Mr John Ellison, duct by Messrs Jonathan Taylor and Bert Plumpton, seleztions by Mr Richard Scarisbriek, with Judy and his flute,also a stump speech; readings by Mr Drinkwater and Mr Llewellyn, and a song by Mr Plimpton. The room was beautifully decorated with fruits, flowers, vegetables, corn, Sm., by a willing band of young ladies and gentle- men, to whom Mr,Llewellyn moved a vote of Macke. Mr Howard seconded the ;motion, which was heartily agreed to.

div.head: CAMDEN HARVEST FESTIVAL SERVICES.
div.p: CAMDEN HARVEST FESTIVAL SERVICES.

The annual barvest thanksgiving services were held at Camden Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn, on 'Sunday and Monday evenings. The chapel was very tastefully decorated. The preacher was the Rev J B Foster. After the service on Monday evening the fruit and vegetables were Fold on behalf of the poor fund, A czlYee supper WM also provided. EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN CHURCH.

Thanksgiving services in connection with the ingather- log of the be roest, were hrld in the Wesleyan 'Church on Sunday, 'The interior of the church was prettily and profusely decorated with fruit, Powers and vegetables, the work having been carried out by the lady members Of the congregation. The preacher for the day was the Bev J Benson, of Crewe, who delivered a couple of aPpropriate discourses, and the choir rendered suitable 115Mr0 and anthems. In the afternOon the choir ren- dered tbe cantata "Two Seasons." There was a large congregatiou,and the solos and choruses were excellently F unE!. The principal soloists were Messrs Fl' Clare. .1 Barr and J Sudworth, Misses Berry, Adams, Barr, 0) Clare, L Barr, D Roberts and Mrs C filipwood. Mr T Clare conducted and Mr G Kidd officiated at the mean. The Peevices vete continued on Monday night-, when the Rev J Smittri of Leigh, occupied the pulpit. On Tuesday evening a social gathering was hid in the Lecture Hall, when there was a sale of fruit In aid of the PUN' fund. Songs were rendered at intervals by Miss Adams, Miss 0 Roberts and Miss Barr.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY_ SEPTEMBER 19, 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY_ SEPTEMBER 19, 1902
EARLESTOWN & NEWTON'
ARRIVAL OF THE NEW FIRE ENGINE.

The new steam flea engine ordered from Messrs Merryweather and Co., by the Newton District Council was delivered at Eaeestown on Wednesday afternoon: It is intended to stable it at the Gas Works, but it is to be hoped the occasions on which it will be used, will be very rare indeed.
EXTRAORDINARY INCIDENT ON NEWTON-LE- WILLOWS STATION.

An extraordinary scene was witnessed on Newton-le-Willows Station on Friday night. Wheia the nine o'clock express train from Liverpool to Manchester drew into the station two men were seen to be struggling together. On the train coming to a standstill they continued their fight on the platform, one of them having got the other down. A crowd of passengers soon gathered round the combatants, who would not desist until they had been separated by the guard and a porter. From the explanations that were given it appeared that a violentquarrel arose in the corn r:-...artment between the men, whose names could not be ascertained, One aeons ed the other of having pulled out a knife, but this was emphatically denie d. Ultimately the men resumed the journey toM =nchester on different trains.
NEWTON ST. PETER'S BIBLF, CL.

On Saturday the male and female members of this class had their annual picnic. Flrty-seven members accompanied it, leaving Newton in waggonettes at half-past one, their destination being Arley Park and Great Budworth. The former place was reached after a pleasurable drive about 4 o'clock, and the !Any was conducted through the grounds and gardens, which were much admired At 5 o'clock all got aboard the waggonettes again for Great Budworah. where an excellent tea was provided and heartily enjoyed. After tea the remainder of the evening was spent in -rambling about the village, and n start for home was made at 8.30. Newton being reached at 11 °Volt. The arrangements, which were efficiently carried out, were in the hands of Mr. J 11 Lane. EARLESTOWN THURSDAY HALF-HOLIDAY FOOTBALL CLITB

- On Wednesday evening a social gathering took place in the Town Hall, Earlestown in connection with this club, occasion being taken to present the cup and medals won by the club last season in the Birkenhead and Dimrict Half-Holiday League. Mr T Bowes presided over the initial proceedings, sup- ported by Mr L Forster, and Mr Hargreaves, secre- tary of the league. There was a large number present and much interest wee evinced in the proceedings. The Chairman gave a brief outline of the club's career, leading up to the winning of the cup and the medals and eulogised in felicitous terms the generosity of the club for charitable purposes. Mr Hargreaves, ' the secre- tary of the League said that last season the Earles- town club played 16 matches, won 11, drew 3. and lost 2. and scored 43 goals against their opponents 23. Mrs L Forster then formally presented the club with the cup and medals. Mr II Pritchard as secretary, also -received a medal. Dancing was afterwards indulged in to the strains of Mr Peplow's string band and was kept up with spirit until about 2.30 on Thursday morning. Messrs Duke, Walton, Hockenbull and Owen officiated as M .C.'s.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLES FOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLES FOWN.
BY A CORRESPONDEN T] .

7he common question is exciting considerable interest in Earlestown and the action of the Dis- trict Council unfavourably commented upon. If there was an election of Councillors, I am afraid the candidates would be asked some awkward questions. This applies more particularly to candi- dates for re-election. It is felt that the Coun- cil have deliberately forfeited the rights pf the public. There may not be any evi- dence that the Common belongs to the people,but on the other hand,bave the Council ever tested Lord Newton's right to it. We are completely in the dark over the matter, and we are likely to remain so if some of the Councillors are to have their way. They seem to forget that they are only the representatives of the people, but they express their own personal views and not the views of their constituents on this question. Why should not we know the contents of the correspoiVence which has passed. Surely we are as capable of passing an opinion upon it as any member of the Council. What footpaths have been bartered away ? This is a question we should hare answered; and have the Council the legal right to Close any footpath which has once ben declared a public footpath ?

The Earlestown Football Club had the simplest task set them on Saturday, which they will pro- bably have any time during the season. They had to meet White Star Wanderers in the qualifying round of the Lancashire Cup, and they simply did as they pleased with the Liverpool men; 12 goals to 1 was the result, but it must not be supposed that as a club Earlestown are so much superior to White Star Wanderers. The latter were awkwardly fixed They had to play a Combination match and conse- quently they only sent a scratch team to Earles- town, with the inevitable result that it was a most uninteresting game from start to finish'

It is not likely Earlestown will have such an easy thing to-morrow, when they meet St. Helens at St. Helens in an English Cup tie. It is to be hoped, however, that they will ha able to secure victory.
Newton, after severely trouncing Tranmere Rovers. had lamt week to succumb o the itnnortuui- ties of Coirk, to the extent of 4 goals to 2.

div.head: WATER POLO.
div.p: WATER POLO.
Liverpool and District League.

WIGLX VST HELF::lll,—Owing to the suspension of the Fit Helens Baths, the first and second teams of Wlgan.and St Helens met at Preston on Thursday night. The reserve teams first took the water, and though defending the deep end and being hard pressed, St Helens. thanks to fine goal keeping by Turner. kept Wigan from scoring in the first half. Interval :—No scores Immediately on resuming. Hazelden gyred for Wigan, Green equalised, and Barr put St Helens ahead: Result s—St Helens Second, two goals; Wigan Second. one. Bxciternent ran high as the first learns took the water. Playing towards the deep end, Wigan pressed, and Smith scored, Swift following with another from close quarters. Manning was kept busy, and at the other end Sharrock beat Peaeock with a shot which struck the inside of the upright. Play ruled fast, and Smith scored a third for Wigan, Swift quickly following with a fourth. Interval :—Wigan four goals ; St Helene, one. Resuming, Smith supplanted Peacock in goal Wigan again pressed, and outplayed their opponents. Pea- cock putting them still further ahead. Immediately afterwards Saunders placed the issue beyond doubt by souring a sixth. Result :—Wigan, seven goals ; St Helens, two.

div.head: RUNCORN'S ACTIVE SERVICE VOLUNTEERS. Thanksgiving Service at the Parish Church
div.p: RUNCORN'S ACTIVE SERVICE VOLUNTEERS. Thanksgiving Service at the Parish Church

Twenty-three VoTura( era and Yeomen went out from Runcorn on active service during the war. Before the first section left a service was held in the Parish Church to bid them farewell and ask God's blessing upon them. Of the 23 men not one was hat. Ore was invalided home, and four bad enteric lover, but they all recovered and are now in good health. No one was wounded. When the Vicat,the Rev Canon Maitland Wood,returned home from a holiday recently be was informed that the Volunteers had asked the churchwardens to arrange for a special service of thankegiving for the safe return of the men. The Vicar readily gave his consent and the service wal held in the Parish Church on Sunday morning. The local Volunteer com- panies paraded at the Drill Hall and accompanied the active service men to the church. The companies were under the command of Captain Ashton,and were headed by the baiad.Arrived at the church the active service men who wore their khaki uniforms,were accommodated with seats at the front. There was a largeh congregation The special prayer issued by the Chaplain-General Biebop Taylor Smith, approved by the Archbishop of Canterbary, and circulated by the Bishop of Chester, wee used, and in the get eral tharksgiving there was a I special recital recital setting forth the cause of the ser- vice. Thanksgiving hymns and the anthem " I will give thanks " (57th Psalm) were sung. The singing was most commendable. Mr Doraston presided at the organ Canon Wood preach ed frcm the text" I will come wit. the mighty acts of the Lord God. I will make trenie h of The righteousness even ot Thine only." Psalm7in verse 13 (revised version). The theme of the etrmo, was the goodness and usefuir ees of thankegivirg.

div.head: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
[l3y °valid.]

Thouh the season is hardly yet in full swing the new touch rule is generally and heartily condemned by the supporters of almost every club in the League. A couple of matches have, in most cases, sufficed to con- vince the most optimistic that the alteration is the most retrograde step ever taken in the history of Northern Union football. When the rule as to the scrimmaging ten yards from touch became law, I remarked in this column that it might or might not tend to more open play. If clubs were content to merely substitute the scrimmage for the punt out, then possibly there would be more open play and the desire of the legislators be gratified. But this is not the way the majority of players look at the matter. They see in the new rule an easy way of work- ing up field by the obsolete method of punting into touch at every opportunity. 'or the backs this is quite a parlour game, but it means horse-work to the forwards, and la severe attack of home-sickness to the spectators. The dreadful days of " scrum,lscrum, scrum " are back again and members are already re- gretting their purchase of season tickets.

Last Saturday, in the opening match at Warrington, the crowd was treated to a beggarly win by a solitary try after a game containing over 100 scrummages. Naturally the treat was not productive of that all-round enthusiasm whichione expects to see at the opening of the season. anind the Warrington-Brighouse match was not, according to reports, the worst! There were even more scrums in the Huddersfield-St. Helens encounter, while Runcorn and Bradford, I believe, scrummaged until the forwards on both sides were quite dizzy with holding their heads down so long. Oh! this eternal scrummaging is horrible to contemplate, and 'tis no wonder that a mov>has already been made to revert to the punt-out or afiything that will restore the bright- ness and the variety of the Northern Rugby gome.

The Champion Club has lead the way in the matter, and it will be interesting to find what replies are made to the following appeal sent out to League clubs by the Broughton Rangers' President and Secretary, Messrs J E Kirkham and F N Fearnley : . . . . . . .

We respectfully beg to invite your opinion as to the merits or success.of the new rule relating to touch play which has caused the abolition of the punt-out from touch. We find in our district that the altera- tion has caused a great amount of dissatisfaction both to the players and spectators. The forward players especially complain of the extraordinary number of scrummages which are entailed by the frequent usage of the touch line by the backs. With- out wishing to appear premature in our judgment on the alteration, we do not consider that there is suffi-

cient merit in the new condition to warrant its existence, and we sincerely believe that the very best interests of the game and Union will be served by straight away reverting back to the rule in force last season. The alteration, we believe, has caused the game to be slower, duller, and much less interesting to the public, and has created a great obstacle to open and scientific play. We should be glad to receive the opinion of your board in the matter, as it is our intention provided that our views are in accord with those of a majority of the clubs, to bring the question before the parent body, whom we ieel sure will give the fullest consideration to this most important matter.

This is a strightforward way of dealing with the matter, and though it seems, almost too much to expect the Union to go back on its own ruling so soon, yet they may find public opinion too strong to be resisted or ignored. There is an astonishing amount of feeling in regard to the new rule already among players and spectators alike, for,whatever the demerits of the punt- out—and there were faults to be found here—it was an imcomparably better rule for the game than the one now in force. The feeling of disgust is as strong in Warrington as anywhere, and I fully expect that the club will support the Rangers in their prompt and praiseworthy action.

There are several serious drawbacks to the new touch rule and the war it operates, apart from the number of ocrummages. There are p'enty of forwards who will soon be playing the waiting game, knowing that how- ever hard they run in the direction of the man carrying the ball, they have little chance of collaring him in possession. The reason, of course, is obvious. Unless a back is close on to his opponents' line he will not attempt to run the ball along the field, when he can make up the ground with greater certainty by kicking into touch. If a forward does go after the back who has possession of the ball, he has all his trouble for naught, and he has the additional trouble of travelling back to the place where the scrummage is formed. Meanwhile the backs are enjoying something almost equal to a siesta. What a rule!

There are several curious things told of the divers effects of the new rule. One is that linesmen are now entitled to more pay than referees in proportion to the amount of work they have to do. Three-quarters are credited with saying that they do not need to get hot in a game, the forwards do all the chasing about necessary Annthe latter —one I know of—are wishing they had the inventor of the new rule in the centre of the scrum. Last, but not least, I hear that Sam Houghton of Run- corn counts himself ten years younger in consequence of the change. He will guarantee to find touch for the "Linnets as long as ever it is necessary!

A Manchester correspondent has summed up the pre- vailing opinion of the general public on the working of the new touch rule, in the following terse and amusing diary. My summary of new touch rule : Monday,September B.—Read that there were nearly 100 scrums in the Runcorn match. Friday, September 12.—Having had a lot of dis- cussion on the matter, decide to see for myself. Saturday, September 13.—Attend Swinton and carefully book every "scrum." Total : let half, 70 ; 2nd, 88. Go away trying to calculate how many minutes' football I paid for. Monday —Purchased season ticket for Hyde-road G. S.L. P.S.—Have since obtained two more converts.

Warrington gained their first brace of points in the League tourney on Saturday when they defeated " Briggus '—the " wooden spoonists " of last year's competition. The margin of one try to nil was much smaller than many anticipated, but up to within a few minutes of the close of the match it looked as though there would be no margin at all. The game was a very close one in more senses than one Scrummages were the order of the day lam assured on reliable authority that there were 48 ' scrums in the first thirty-five minutes of the game and 53 in the second. That works out at an average of more than one scrumma,e per minute ! No wonder there was little scoring. To say that the match was a disappointing one to the specta- tors is to put it mildly. At the outset they were called upon `to endure three-quarters of an how's painful waiting on a bleak field for the visitors to put in an appearance, and they were afterwards entertained to an exhibition of how the punt into touch rule can be made to destroy all interest in the game.

Of the game itself, little more need be said. Now and again, the Warrington backs showed a little com- bined play, but the wing men were generally found in the wrong place, and on two occasions Fish overran Hockenhall before the ball was passed. There was a lack of cohesion and understanding among the backs and at present their standard of play is below that of a year ago when they were more strenuously worked in consequence of the punt out rule. Harris is the only player who has scored this season and for last Satur- day's try he is indebted to F Swift for a timely pass when the game seemed likely to end in a pointless draw,

Up to the present Knight has successfully filled the position of full back The committee have been fortunate in finding such a capable substitute, pending their difficulty with Hallam, a difficulty which, it is hoped, will soon be settled. Ratcliffe is still on the injured list.

The visitors seemed content to aim at making a draw og the match and it wa4 a sore disappointment to them when Harris dashed their hopes in this direction by scoring in the last few minutes. Prior to this happen- ing, Hartley and Crowther found touch with great regularity, and the ire of the spectators was thoroughly roused when the ball was occasionally kicked over the pavilion into an adjoining field. Before the match was over, many spectators were wending their way home-. wards, vexed and disgusted with the display, if such it can be called.

The Warrington Committee have selected the same team as last Saturday to do duty in the match at St. Ilelens to-day. There should be additional interest lent to the encounter from the fact that the two tea are destined to meet in the first round of the cup com- petition. This should really be a fairly safe engage- ment for Warrington, but on present form they will be distinctly fortunate to get the better of the Saints. I am quite confident they will lose if the touch-line is resorted to in the same idiotic fashion as it was last Saturday. Even if the:Saints punt persistently into touch, Warrington should not follow suit, for with a speedy set of backs and only moderate forwards they will do better to keep the game open at all costs short of throwing an advantage away. The backs must bear this in mind or they will be on the wrong side of the fence when the final is sounded to-day.
There Is some mis apprehension among the Warring ton members. Many of them imagine that their mem bers' tickets are not available for the cup tie games

Their alarm is unnecessary however. All bona-Ado members are entitled to free admission. It is only the holders of season-tickets who do not carry the privi- leges of membership—such as are issued by some of the leading clubs—who will have to pay when the cup ties commence. Bona-fide members like those of the Warrington club are absolutely safe in this respect.

Mr Frank Sugg, the well-known sports outfitter, of 32, Lord-street, Liverpool, has issued his football cata- logue, and clubs in need of requisites of any description would do well to consult this handy publication. Both Mr Sugg and his brother are thoroughly practical sportsmen, having a splendid record as footballers and cricketers. The specialities mentioned in the catalogue include " The football king " ball which has been used in thirty international matches, and in six English cup finals. It should be noted that Mr Suggs' football shirts and clothing generally, are manufactured on the premises, and that a rapidly increasing trade for foot- ball shirts and clothing alone has necessitated the lay- ing of new plant and an electric motor.
Cycling.

It is becoming evident that immediate attention should be given to the renovation of danger and caution boards up and down the country says "Cycling." From a number of correspondents we have received letters pointing out that the wording on a large number of boards they have come across are absolutely unreadable and useless. One of the most recent fatalities gives a strong case in point. It will be remembered that Mr EW T Richmond met with a terrible accident at Trevyn Hill, near Land's End, sus- taining severe injuries, and he died at the end of last week. At the West Penwith Rural District Council meetin, held last 'week, questions were asked as to the state of the hill. The Rev T Bennett, vicar of St Levan, said there was no sign-board on the Treen side of the road. There was on the other but it needed repainting, and it is reported that the surveyor also added that the board was in a very mbad condition. The clerk thought that they should see that the C.T.O kept the boards in orderer took them down. Thus it will be seen from the remarks of the Council that the board was not very legible. A Cornish reader writes that it is high time that some of the boards in his neighbourhood were renewed. He specifies one board on which the painlwas "weathered " away, leaving only hierogly- phics. There is, too, he adds, a broken notice on the top of the hill leading into Perranporth, this being a very dangerous lull; and many other hills in his district really require dagger-boards. We must say that upon those bodies who have erected these boards a grave re- sponsibility rests, and it is their duty to either renovate , the boards or to remove them. To fulfil their purpose they should be kept in order and the district representa- tives be made fully alive to the great danger attached Ito any omission in this respect At the inquest on Mr Richmond the jury added a rider urging that a warning board be placed on the lull.

I Louis Michael, the Welsh midget, after several futile PO ,sons as a jockey,has again taken on with his old lave. Oa Suuday week, at the Velodrome du Par; des Princes, he signalised his return to the path by beatirg his fellow-countryman Tom Linton's one hour record of 45 miles 1,034 yards, covcrieg the remarkable distance of 46 miles 1,360 yards in the time. Ties feat was done ia a race, agailet ouch tried men as Lesaa. of 13rdeaux-Paris f.rne,Jicquelin,theonce-farnous sprinter Houhours, a proved middle-distance man, and Contenet. The last-named is a new man, but he proved a thorn in Michael's side, gamely sticking Co the Welshman for the best part of the first twenty miles. Indeed at one part of the race he V 71.9 well ahead of Michael, but, tailing off afterwards, he was ultimately beaten for second place by &labours, who finished abont half a mile behind Michael. The event was witnessed by 18,000 people—a large crowd even for Paris. Michael, lit is intereqing to note, was paced by a tandem. bicycle of 14-horse power, and of course the machiue was fitted with wind shields. One would like to see what A A Chase could do under similar conditions. His best pacing inacbiao is a single bicycle of seven-horse power. We believe that he objects to wind shields, deeming them artifici 11, and that it is for this resson he does not race in Parii'. It seems that now some of the French share his objection, for it is stated ti;at in future they will not b? sae we I on tle ['arc des Princes track. One fancies, however, that if the authorities of the Velodrome Buffalo—the opposition track—do not fall into line, and that should Michael s seat be improved on that track, the proprietors of the Pare des Princeo will readily revoke their decision.
